Power BI service — export an interactive report to PDF
Power BI Desktop — create a multi-page report using multiple report pages
Power BI Desktop — use the visual-level page breaks feature
explanation: Paginated reports (.rdl) built with Power BI Report Builder are designed for controlled, pixel-perfect printed output. They support repeating page headers, explicit page breaks, and tables that span multiple pages — features not available in standard Power BI Desktop reports.
choiceExplanations: Correct. Power BI Report Builder creates paginated .rdl reports designed for pixel-perfect controlled printing with repeating headers and multi-page tables.
Exporting an interactive report to PDF creates a snapshot of each canvas page as-is. It doesn't reflow content, add repeating page headers, or handle tables that span across controlled print pages.
Power BI Desktop creates interactive canvas reports. There's no concept of print pages — visuals don't automatically paginate across a controlled number of printed pages with repeating headers.
Standard Power BI Desktop reports don't have a built-in page break feature for visuals. The visual canvas doesn't produce the structured, repeating-header print layout that paginated reports provide.

examObjective: Visualize and analyze data > Natural language analytics
commonTrap: Confusing Q&A with Smart Narratives or Quick Insights
question: A business user wants to type natural language questions like 'total sales by region last year' into a Power BI report and have visuals generated automatically. Which feature enables this?
choices: Q&A visual
Smart narratives
Auto-generated summaries
Quick insights
explanation: The Q&A visual lets users type natural language questions. Power BI interprets the query using the model's field names and synonyms and generates the most appropriate visual automatically. It supports self-service exploration without requiring report design skills.

choiceExplanations.0: Correct. The Q&A visual accepts typed natural language questions and generates the most appropriate visual automatically.
choiceExplanations.1: Smart narratives automatically generate text summaries describing notable patterns in a visual's data. They produce computer-generated text — users don't type queries into them.
choiceExplanations.2: 'Auto-generated summaries' is not a distinct Power BI feature. It partially describes smart narratives, which don't accept user-typed natural language questions.
choiceExplanations.3: Quick insights is a Power BI service feature that automatically scans a dataset and suggests visualizations. It runs automatically — users don't type questions to drive it.

examObjective: Visualize and analyze data > Advanced visual features
commonTrap: Manually duplicating visuals instead of small multiples
question: You want to display a separate line chart for each product category, all sharing the same axes and scale for comparison, without manually duplicating visuals. Which Power BI feature should you use?
choices: Apply a 'split by' slicer that regenerates the chart per selection
Create one chart per category and align them on the canvas by hand
Use a matrix visual with line chart sparklines
Use small multiples in the visual's format settings
explanation: Small multiples automatically create a grid of the same visual type — one instance per value of a chosen field. All instances share the same axes and scale, making cross-category comparison straightforward without manual duplication.
choiceExplanations: A slicer filters the existing visual to show one selected category at a time. It shows one category per selection — not all categories simultaneously for side-by-side comparison.

Manually creating and aligning separate visuals doesn't scale when categories are dynamic. You'd need to update every visual individually when data changes, and maintaining consistent axes is a constant challenge.
Matrix sparklines show tiny inline trend lines within table cells — compact but not full-sized, independently readable charts with shared axes.
Correct. Small multiples create a grid of the same visual type — one per category value — all sharing axes for easy comparison.

examObjective: Visualize and analyze data > Cross-page filtering
commonTrap: Copying/pasting slicers thinking they auto-sync
question: Your report has 3 pages and you want a Region slicer selection made on any page to filter all 3 pages simultaneously. How do you achieve this?
choices: Add Region as a report-level filter in the Filters pane
Use Sync Slicers — configure sync and visibility for the slicer across all target pages
Copy and paste the slicer onto every page — pasted slicers sync automatically
Publish the slicer to a shared panel in the Power BI service
explanation: The Sync Slicers pane (View > Sync Slicers) lets you configure which pages a slicer synchronizes with and is visible on. When synced, a selection on any page updates all synced pages simultaneously.
choiceExplanations: A report-level filter applies a fixed filter set by the report author. Users cannot interactively change it like a slicer — it's author-controlled, not user-controlled.
Correct. Sync Slicers (View > Sync Slicers) configures a slicer to synchronize and optionally be visible across specified pages.
Copying and pasting creates independent slicer instances. Selecting a value on one page's slicer doesn't update pasted slicers on other pages — they look identical but function independently.
There is no 'shared filter panel' feature in the Power BI service for syncing slicers across pages. This option describes a non-existent feature.

examObjective: Visualize and analyze data > Financial visualization
commonTrap: Using stacked bar instead of waterfall for cumulative flow
question: A financial report needs to show how different revenue streams and cost categories combine to produce final net profit — visualizing each positive contribution and each deduction from a starting value. Which visualization is most appropriate?
choices: 100% stacked column chart
Funnel chart
Stacked bar chart
Waterfall chart
explanation: A waterfall chart shows how individual positive and negative values contribute to a cumulative running total — ideal for financial bridge charts. Stacked bars show composition but not cumulative flow. A funnel chart represents stage-by-stage drop-off, not financial contributions.
choiceExplanations: A 100% stacked column chart shows proportional composition (each bar sums to 100%). It's for comparing proportions across categories, not for showing absolute values in a cumulative flow.

A funnel chart represents stage-by-stage count drop-off in a sequential process (like a sales pipeline). It shows conversion reduction through stages, not financial contributions to a net profit total.

A stacked bar chart shows how components make up a total at a point in time. It doesn't show the sequential additive flow from a starting value to a net result — you can't see how one value leads to the next.
Correct. A waterfall chart shows cumulative positive and negative contributions from a starting value to a net result — ideal for financial bridge analysis.

examObjective: Model the data > CALCULATE and filter context
commonTrap: Thinking SUM alone or SUMX ignores slicer context
question: A report page has a {dimension} slicer. A KPI card must always show the grand total across ALL {dimension}s, regardless of the slicer selection. Which measure achieves this?
choices: Total = CALCULATE(SUM(Fact[Amount]), ALL(Dim[DimName]))
Total = SUM(Fact[Amount])
Total = TOTALYTD(SUM(Fact[Amount]), Dates[Date])
Total = SUMX(Fact, Fact[Amount])
explanation: CALCULATE with ALL() removes the filter context imposed by the slicer, forcing the measure to evaluate across all dimension values. SUM and SUMX without CALCULATE still respect the active filter context.
choiceExplanations: Correct. CALCULATE with ALL() clears any filters on the dimension table, so the measure evaluates across all dimension values regardless of the slicer.
SUM without CALCULATE still evaluates inside the current filter context. The slicer adds a filter to the visual, so SUM will only total rows matching the selected dimension value.
TOTALYTD is a time intelligence function for year-to-date aggregation along a date axis. It has no effect on non-date slicers like department or region.
SUMX iterates rows but does not modify filter context. Like SUM, it still respects the active slicer filter without CALCULATE wrapping it.
daxExpression:
-- A KPI card must always show grand total regardless of slicer
Grand Total =
    CALCULATE(
        SUM(Fact[Amount]),
        ALL(Dim[DimName])   -- removes the slicer filter
    )

examObjective: Model the data > Iterator functions
commonTrap: Using SUM(A)*SUM(B) instead of SUMX for row-level multiplication
question: An HR analyst needs a measure that calculates total annual compensation cost. Each employee has a MonthlySalary and a BonusRate. The formula per employee is: MonthlySalary * 12 * (1 + BonusRate). Which DAX measure is correct?
choices: Annual Cost = SUM(Employees[MonthlySalary]) * 12 * (1 + AVERAGE(Employees[BonusRate]))
Annual Cost = CALCULATE(SUM(Employees[MonthlySalary]) * 12, ALL(Employees[BonusRate]))
Annual Cost = SUM(Employees[MonthlySalary]) + SUM(Employees[BonusRate])
Annual Cost = SUMX(Employees, Employees[MonthlySalary] * 12 * (1 + Employees[BonusRate]))
explanation: SUMX iterates over every row in the Employees table, applying the per-row formula using each employee's actual MonthlySalary and BonusRate. Option A incorrectly uses AVERAGE(BonusRate), which loses the per-employee variation and produces a different (wrong) total.
choiceExplanations: This approach multiplies the total salary by the average bonus rate — incorrect because each employee has a different bonus rate. The weighted average approach produces a different result from summing individual calculations.
CALCULATE does not help here. Removing filters from BonusRate does not enable row-level multiplication across two columns simultaneously.
This simply adds salary to bonus rate — units are incompatible (currency vs percentage) and the formula logic is completely wrong.
Correct. SUMX iterates row by row, evaluating MonthlySalary * 12 * (1 + BonusRate) for each individual employee using their actual values.
daxExpression:
Annual Cost =
    SUMX(
        Employees,
        Employees[MonthlySalary] * 12 * (1 + Employees[BonusPct])
    )

-- Iterates each employee row, computes their annual cost,
-- then sums across all employees.

examObjective: Model the data > Time intelligence
commonTrap: Using DATESYTD (year-to-date) instead of DATESQTD (quarter-to-date)
question: A bank needs a measure showing total deposits accumulated from the start of the current quarter to the selected date. The model has a marked Date table. Which measure is correct?
choices: QTD Deposits = CALCULATE(SUM(Deposits[Amount]), FILTER(Dates, Dates[Quarter] = QUARTER(TODAY())))
QTD Deposits = SUMX(DATESINPERIOD(Dates[Date], TODAY(), -90, DAY), SUM(Deposits[Amount]))
QTD Deposits = CALCULATE(SUM(Deposits[Amount]), DATESYTD(Dates[Date]))
QTD Deposits = TOTALQTD(SUM(Deposits[Amount]), Dates[Date])
explanation: TOTALQTD is the time intelligence function for quarter-to-date totals. It is equivalent to CALCULATE with DATESQTD. Option A uses DATESYTD which returns year-to-date, not quarter-to-date. Option C uses a 90-day rolling window which does not align to calendar quarter boundaries.
choiceExplanations: QUARTER(TODAY()) returns a number (1-4), but comparing Dates[Quarter] requires that column to exist with the same format. More importantly, this filter does not reset at the selected date within the quarter — it includes all dates in the quarter.
DATESINPERIOD with -90 days creates a 90-day rolling window. Q1 has 90 days, but Q2 has 91, Q3 has 92, and Q4 has 92 — so this does not align correctly to quarter boundaries.
DATESYTD returns dates from the start of the YEAR to the current date — not the start of the quarter. This would give year-to-date totals, not quarter-to-date.
Correct. TOTALQTD(SUM(Deposits[Amount]), Dates[Date]) calculates the sum from the start of the current quarter to the selected date.
daxExpression:
QTD Deposits = TOTALQTD(SUM(Deposits[Amount]), Dates[Date])

-- TOTALQTD accumulates from the first day of the current quarter
-- to the last date in the current filter context.
-- Resets at the start of each new quarter (Q1: Jan 1, Q2: Apr 1, etc.)

examObjective: Manage and secure Power BI > Dynamic RLS
commonTrap: Using USERNAME() which returns DOMAIN\username format, not email
question: A manufacturing company has 8 plant managers. Each manager should see production data only for their plant. The Plants dimension table has a ManagerEmail column storing each manager's Azure AD email. Which DAX filter expression correctly implements dynamic RLS?
choices: [ManagerEmail] = LOOKUPVALUE(Plants[ManagerEmail], Plants[PlantID], SELECTEDVALUE(Plants[PlantID]))
[ManagerEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()
[ManagerEmail] = USERNAME()
[ManagerEmail] = CUSTOMDATA()
explanation: USERPRINCIPALNAME() returns the authenticated user's UPN, which matches their Azure AD email address (e.g., jane@contoso.com). USERNAME() returns the Windows identity format DOMAIN\username, which does not match email addresses stored in the table.
choiceExplanations: LOOKUPVALUE without a dynamic user context returns the selected value from a slicer, not the authenticated user's identity. This would not restrict data by the current logged-in user.
Correct. USERPRINCIPALNAME() returns the Azure AD UPN (e.g., jane@contoso.com), which matches the email format stored in the ManagerEmail column.

USERNAME() returns the Windows identity in DOMAIN\username format (e.g., CONTOSO\jane). This does not match email addresses stored in columns like ManagerEmail, so no rows would be returned for cloud-based Power BI service.

CUSTOMDATA() reads an optional custom string passed via the connection string. It requires the application layer to inject the value and is used in embedded scenarios, not standard Power BI Service RLS.

examObjective: Prepare the data > Combining queries
commonTrap: Confusing Append (stack rows) with Merge (join columns)
question: A retail company has three branch stores, each exporting a Sales table with identical columns: OrderID, Date, Amount, ProductID. You need one unified Sales table in Power BI. What should you do in Power Query?
choices: Reference one query and write a UNION M expression
Merge the three queries using a left outer join on OrderID
Append the three queries to stack all rows into one table
Merge the queries then unpivot the branch columns
explanation: Append combines tables with the same column structure by stacking rows vertically — exactly the requirement here. Merge performs a horizontal join matching rows by a key column, which would attempt to join sales records rather than combine them.
choiceExplanations: UNION is a DAX table function used in calculated tables, not a Power Query M function. In M the equivalent is Table.Combine, but using the Append Queries UI is the correct standard approach.

Merge performs a horizontal JOIN — it tries to match rows between tables by a key column. Merging three identical Sales tables on OrderID would create a wide table with duplicate column sets, not a combined list of all sales.
Correct. Append stacks tables with identical schemas vertically, producing a single unified table with all rows from all three branches.
Merge followed by unpivot is a complex multi-step workaround that would produce incorrect results for combining identical-schema tables.

expectedOutput.label: After Append All Three — unified Sales table (6 rows)

examObjective: Prepare the data > Storage modes and connectivity
commonTrap: Choosing Import mode thinking scheduled refresh is fast enough for near-real-time data
question: An operations team monitors IoT sensor data that updates every 30 seconds. The Power BI dashboard must always show the current equipment status. The dataset grows by approximately 50,000 rows per day with no upper size limit. Which connectivity mode should you use?
choices: Dual mode to combine cached and live data
DirectQuery to always query the source database directly
Live connection to an existing on-premises Analysis Services model
Import mode with a 30-minute scheduled refresh
explanation: DirectQuery sends queries directly to the source each time a visual loads, ensuring the data is always current. Import mode refreshes on a schedule (minimum 30 minutes for Power BI Pro), which cannot satisfy a 30-second freshness requirement.
choiceExplanations: Dual mode is designed for dimension tables in composite models, allowing them to serve both cached and live queries. It is not a solution for near-real-time fact data requirements.
Correct. DirectQuery does not import or cache data — every visual render queries the source database directly, ensuring the dashboard always reflects the latest sensor readings.
Live connection requires an existing Analysis Services or Power BI dataset. It does not apply to a source database directly, and freshness depends on SSAS refresh schedules.
Power BI Pro allows a maximum of 8 refreshes per day (every 30 minutes). Premium allows up to 48 refreshes per day (every 30 minutes). Neither satisfies a 30-second data freshness requirement.

examObjective: Prepare the data > Query performance optimization
commonTrap: Thinking rename and filter operations break query folding
question: You build a Power Query transformation against SQL Server with these steps in order: (1) Filter rows where Status = "Active", (2) Rename three columns, (3) Add a custom column using Text.BetweenDelimiters(). Which statement about query folding is correct?
choices: Query folding only applies to whole-table imports, not filtered queries
Steps 1 and 2 fold to SQL; step 3 breaks query folding and all subsequent steps run in-memory
Only step 1 folds; renaming columns already breaks query folding
All three steps fold to SQL — Power Query translates M functions to T-SQL automatically
explanation: Filter and rename operations translate directly to SQL (WHERE clause and column aliases). Text.BetweenDelimiters is an M-specific function with no SQL equivalent, so Power Query cannot translate it to a SQL query — folding breaks at that step, and any steps after it also run in-memory.
choiceExplanations: Query folding applies to any query built against a data source that supports it (SQL Server, Oracle, OData, etc.), regardless of filtering. The query is translated to the native query language of the source.
Correct. Filter (WHERE) and rename (alias) are foldable SQL operations. Text.BetweenDelimiters has no SQL equivalent, breaking folding. All steps after the break also execute in-memory.
Column renaming translates to SQL column aliasing and does not break folding. Native database query steps like filter, sort, and rename are typically foldable.
Not all M functions have SQL equivalents. M-specific functions like Text.BetweenDelimiters, List.Contains, and many transformation functions cannot be translated to T-SQL.

tables.name: Steps and folding status
rows: Sent to SQL as WHERE clause
M expression cannot be translated to SQL
Once fold breaks, everything after runs in-memory

examObjective: Model the data > Calculated columns vs measures
commonTrap: Creating a DAX measure thinking it can be used as a slicer source
question: An e-commerce analyst wants to add a profit margin band (Low / Medium / High) to the Products table so that report users can filter visuals using a slicer. Margin band is based on a calculated percentage. What should you create?
choices: A DAX measure that returns the margin band label for each product
A Power BI parameter with Low, Medium, High options
A calculated column in the Products table using a DAX IF/SWITCH expression
A calculated table containing only the three band labels
explanation: Slicers require a physical column stored in a table. Calculated columns are evaluated row-by-row at refresh time and stored in the model — they appear as regular columns and can be used as slicer fields. Measures are evaluated at query time per visual context and cannot be used as slicer sources.
choiceExplanations: Measures are evaluated dynamically per visual context and do not exist as stored column values. They cannot be dragged into a slicer to let users filter by their result.
A Power BI parameter creates a numeric or text input that changes measure behavior — it is not the same as assigning each product to a category band based on its calculated margin.
Correct. A calculated column uses a DAX IF/SWITCH expression evaluated row-by-row at model refresh. The result is stored as a column in the Products table, making it available as a slicer field.

A calculated table with only three rows (Low, Medium, High) would be a disconnected reference table. Without a relationship or row-level assignment, it cannot filter the Products table through a slicer.
daxExpression:
-- Calculated column: assign ProfitMargin band based on margin value
MarginBand =
    SWITCH(
        TRUE(),
        Products[ProfitMargin] < 0.10, "Low",
        Products[ProfitMargin] < 0.25, "Medium",
        "High"
    )

-- Calculated column stores result per row at refresh time.
-- Users can slice/filter by MarginBand like any other column.

expectedOutput.label: Calculated column result per product row

examObjective: Prepare the data > Merge query join types
commonTrap: Using inner join and losing customers with no orders
question: A CRM system has a Customers table and an Orders table. You need a Power Query result that includes ALL customers — including those who have never placed an order — with order details where available and nulls where no orders exist. Which join type should you use in Merge Queries?
choices: Right Outer Join — returns all orders with null customer columns where no match exists
Left Outer Join — returns all customers with null order columns where no match exists
Full Outer Join — returns all rows from both tables with nulls on both sides
Inner Join — returns only customers who have at least one matching order
explanation: Left Outer Join keeps every row from the left (Customers) table and matches against the right (Orders) table. Rows with no matching order get nulls in the order columns. Inner Join would exclude customers with no orders.
choiceExplanations: Right Outer Join preserves all rows from the right (Orders) table. If any orders had a missing customer record, those would be kept. This is the opposite of what is needed.
Correct. Left Outer Join preserves all rows from the left (primary) table — Customers — and fills in nulls for order columns where no matching order exists.
Full Outer Join returns all rows from both tables. While this would include all customers, it would also include any orphaned orders with no customer, which is not what was asked.
Inner Join only returns rows where a match exists in BOTH tables. Customers who have never placed an order would be excluded entirely from the result.

expectedOutput.label: Left Outer Join — all 3 customers, null where no matching order

examObjective: Visualize and analyze data > Bookmarks and button actions
commonTrap: Using page navigation or drill-through instead of bookmarks for show/hide panels
question: A report developer wants to create a collapsible information panel on a dashboard page. Clicking an "Info" button shows a group of explanation visuals; clicking "Close" hides them. The panel and buttons exist on the same report page. What is the correct implementation?
choices: Configure drill-through navigation to a dedicated information page
Create two bookmarks capturing the panel visible and hidden states, then assign them to the Info and Close buttons
Create a report page tooltip that appears when hovering over visuals
Use page navigation buttons to toggle between two separate report pages
explanation: Bookmarks capture the state of a report page — including the visibility of visual groups. By creating one bookmark with the panel visible and another with it hidden, then assigning these bookmarks to button actions, you create a toggle effect without leaving the page.
choiceExplanations: Drill-through navigates from one page to another, passing filter context. It does not show/hide content on the current page and would take the user away from the dashboard.
Correct. Bookmarks freeze the visibility state of visuals and groups. Assigning bookmark actions to buttons allows toggling show/hide of the panel within the same page.
Report page tooltips appear on hover over a specific visual, not on button click. They show supplemental information in a floating panel, not collapsible content within the main canvas.
Page navigation switches the user to an entirely different report page. This would replace the dashboard view rather than showing an overlay panel within it.

examObjective: Visualize and analyze data > Cross-report navigation
commonTrap: Using standard drill-through which only works within the same report file
question: A company has two Power BI reports published to the same workspace: a Procurement Summary report and a Supplier Detail report. Users need to click a supplier name in the Summary report and navigate to the Supplier Detail report with that supplier pre-filtered. What should you configure?
choices: Synchronized slicers shared across both reports
Cross-report drill-through: designate a drill-through page in the Supplier Detail report and enable cross-report drill-through on that page
Bookmark navigation linking to a URL of the Supplier Detail report
Standard drill-through on a detail page inside the Procurement Summary report
explanation: Cross-report drill-through allows navigation from one published report to a drill-through page in another published report within the same workspace. Standard drill-through only works within the same .pbix file. Both reports must be published to the same workspace.
choiceExplanations: Synchronized slicers keep slicer selections consistent across pages in the same report. They do not enable navigation between separate reports or pass filter context across report boundaries.

Correct. Cross-report drill-through requires enabling the setting on the target drill-through page in the Supplier Detail report. Once enabled, any report in the same workspace can drill through to it.

Bookmark navigation within a report cannot pass filter context to another report. URL-based navigation is possible via the Power BI embedded URL format but requires custom development and is not a native report feature.
Standard drill-through creates a detail page within the same .pbix file. It cannot navigate to a separate published report — the drill-through target must exist in the same report file.

examObjective: Model the data > Data model design
commonTrap: Importing the flat table as-is thinking Power BI handles denormalization
question: A manufacturing company has a single flat table called OperationsLog with columns: ProductID, ProductName, CategoryName, SupplierName, SupplierCountry, OrderDate, Quantity, UnitCost. You are building the Power BI model. What is the recommended approach?
choices: Import as-is and create DAX calculated tables for each dimension at query time
Import the flat table as-is; Power BI handles the redundancy with VertiPaq compression
Create a fully normalized snowflake schema with separate tables for Category and Country
Use Power Query to split into a star schema: a fact table (Quantities and Costs) and dimension tables (Product, Supplier, Date)
explanation: Star schema — a central fact table with denormalized dimension tables — is the recommended pattern for Power BI. It reduces model size through VertiPaq compression of repeated string values in dimensions, enables clear relationship paths, and optimizes DAX query performance. Snowflake schemas add unnecessary join complexity.
choiceExplanations: DAX calculated tables created at query time are evaluated on every model refresh and do not benefit from pre-loaded relationships. They add complexity without the modeling benefits of proper Power Query shaping.

While VertiPaq does compress repeated strings, importing a flat denormalized table creates a large model with redundant data, makes relationships impossible, and produces slow measures that must scan all rows.

Snowflake schema adds extra normalization layers (e.g., a separate Category table linked to Product). Power BI performs best with a single denormalized dimension per entity — the extra joins in a snowflake hurt query performance.
Correct. Splitting into a star schema in Power Query creates separate dimension tables (Product, Supplier, Date) and a slim fact table, enabling efficient relationships and fast DAX calculations.

relationshipDiagram.issue: Original flat table had all columns mixed together. Split into one fact table (measures + keys) and separate dimension tables (attributes). This star schema enables efficient filtering and reduces model size.

examObjective: Visualize and analyze data > Paginated report design
commonTrap: Using Power BI Desktop for pixel-perfect, variable-length print documents
question: A company needs to generate customer invoices. Each invoice must have a pixel-perfect header, company logo, and a line item table that expands to fit any number of rows. Invoices must export cleanly to PDF for printing. Some customers have 1 line item; others have 400. Which tool should you use?
choices: Power BI Report Builder — create a paginated report with a tablix data region
Power BI Dashboard — pin tiles to match the invoice structure
Power BI Desktop — create a table visual formatted as the invoice layout
Power BI dataflow — transform the invoice data and export to Excel
explanation: Power BI Report Builder creates paginated reports — documents designed for pixel-perfect, print-optimized output that grows dynamically to fit any number of data rows. They support precise headers, footers, page breaks, and export to PDF/Word/Excel. Standard Power BI reports have fixed canvas sizes and are not designed for variable-length printed documents.
choiceExplanations: Correct. Power BI Report Builder is specifically designed for paginated, print-ready documents. Tablix data regions expand vertically to accommodate any number of rows, with proper page breaks and pixel-precise formatting.
Power BI dashboards are collections of pinned tiles for at-a-glance monitoring. They are not documents, cannot generate print layouts, and do not support variable-length row data.

Power BI Desktop reports use a fixed-size canvas optimized for interactive browsing. Table visuals truncate or scroll rather than creating proper page breaks for printing — not suitable for variable-length printed invoices.
Dataflows are for data transformation and storage in Power BI service — they are not a reporting or document generation tool.

examObjective: Manage and secure Power BI > Dataset refresh optimization
commonTrap: Switching to DirectQuery to solve refresh timeout instead of incremental refresh
question: A transactional database contains 5 years of order history (60 million rows). The table grows by ~15,000 rows daily. Full dataset refreshes take 5 hours and are timing out. Historical data older than 3 years never changes. You need to reduce refresh time while retaining all 5 years of history. What should you configure?
choices: Switch to DirectQuery to eliminate the need for scheduled refreshes entirely
Configure incremental refresh: store 5 years, refresh only the last 7 days of data on each run
Add a date filter in Power Query to import only the current year's data
Split the import into 5 separate annual queries and union them with UNION in DAX
explanation: Incremental refresh partitions the dataset by date range. Historical partitions (older data that never changes) are frozen and never re-imported. Only the recent partition (last 7 days) is refreshed each cycle, reducing a 5-hour job to minutes while retaining the full 5-year history.
choiceExplanations: DirectQuery eliminates refresh latency by querying the source live, but querying 60 million rows interactively without pre-aggregation severely impacts report performance. It solves the refresh problem but creates a worse user experience.

Correct. Incremental refresh partitions data by date. The 5-year historical partitions are frozen and not re-processed. Only the incremental window (last 7 days) refreshes, reducing load dramatically.
A date filter limiting import to the current year loses 4 years of historical data. Users would lose trend analysis and year-over-year comparisons.
Five separate annual import queries still require refreshing all 5 annual queries. UNION in DAX creates a calculated table that is re-evaluated on every refresh, not on an incremental basis.

examObjective: Model the data > Iterator functions
commonTrap: Multiplying column totals instead of per-row values
question: The Sales table shown contains no Revenue column. Which measure correctly calculates total revenue?
choices: AVERAGE(Sales[UnitPrice]) * COUNT(Sales[Qty])
SUM(Sales[Qty]) * SUM(Sales[UnitPrice])
SUMX(Sales, Sales[Qty] * Sales[UnitPrice])
CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Qty]), ALL(Sales[UnitPrice]))
explanation: SUMX iterates each row — multiplying Qty by UnitPrice per row, then summing: (2×500)+(3×50)+(5×20) = 1,250. SUM(Qty)*SUM(Price) gives 10×570 = 5,700, which is mathematically wrong because it cross-multiplies totals.
choiceExplanations: AVERAGE(UnitPrice) × COUNT(Qty) = 190 × 3 = 570. This is an estimate, not actual total revenue — it would only be correct if all products had the same quantity.
SUM(Qty)*SUM(Price) multiplies total quantities (2+3+5=10) by total unit prices (500+50+20=570), giving 5,700. This is wrong — it should multiply per row then sum.
Correct. SUMX iterates each row: Bike=2×500=1,000, Helmet=3×50=150, Gloves=5×20=100. Total = 1,250.
CALCULATE with ALL changes filter context but does not perform per-row multiplication. This expression is logically incorrect for revenue calculation.

examObjective: Model the data > CALCULATE and filter context
commonTrap: Expecting the measure to return only the filtered region's total
question: A report visual is filtered to show only the East region. The [Total All Regions] measure is defined as shown. What value does this measure return in the East row?
choices: 3,500 — all regions except East
1,000 — only the East region sales
BLANK — ALL removes the entire Sales table
4,500 — total across all regions
explanation: CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), ALL(Sales[Region])) removes the Region filter from the current context. The measure can now see all regions regardless of the visual filter: 1,000+2,000+1,500 = 4,500.
choiceExplanations: ALL does not invert or negate the filter — it removes it entirely. The result is the grand total, not the total excluding East.
1,000 would be the result of a plain SUM(Sales[Amount]) without ALL(). The East filter would restrict it. ALL() specifically overrides that filter.
ALL does not remove the entire Sales table — it removes filters on the specified column or table. The expression still evaluates across all rows.
Correct. ALL(Sales[Region]) removes the region filter from context. CALCULATE then evaluates SUM across all 3 regions: 1,000+2,000+1,500 = 4,500.
daxExpression: [Total All Regions] = CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), ALL(Sales[Region]))

examObjective: Model the data > FILTER function
commonTrap: Thinking FILTER returns a scalar value or a count
question: The expression shown is evaluated against the Products table. What does FILTER return?
choices: The value 550 — total Price of Sports products
A BLANK — FILTER cannot be used as a standalone expression
A table containing only the two Sports rows
The number 2 — count of Sports products
explanation: FILTER always returns a table — in this case the subset of Products where Category = 'Sports'. It returns the Bike and Helmet rows. FILTER must be wrapped in an aggregation (COUNTROWS, SUMX, etc.) to produce a scalar value.
choiceExplanations: Summing prices requires SUMX(FILTER(...), Products[Price]). FILTER returns a table of rows — not an aggregated value.
FILTER is a valid table function and returns a real table, not BLANK. It is commonly passed as the first argument to SUMX, COUNTROWS, and CALCULATE.
Correct. FILTER(Products, Products[Category] = "Sports") returns a table with Bike (Sports, 500) and Helmet (Sports, 50). The result shown is the expected table output.
Counting rows requires COUNTROWS(FILTER(...)). FILTER on its own returns the matching rows as a table, not a count.
daxExpression: FILTER(Products, Products[Category] = "Sports")

examObjective: Prepare the data > Pivot and Unpivot
commonTrap: Confusing Pivot with Unpivot direction
question: The source table (Before) must be transformed into the normalized format shown (After). Which Power Query step produces this result?
choices: Transpose the entire table
Pivot the Quarter column
Unpivot the Q1, Q2, and Q3 columns
Group By Product and sum the columns
explanation: Unpivoting Q1, Q2, Q3 converts each column header into an Attribute row value and each cell into a Value row value. This normalizes the wide table into the row-per-quarter format that Power BI's columnar model expects.
choiceExplanations: Transpose flips rows and columns globally. It would make Products into column headers and quarters into row indices — not the format shown.
Pivot expands rows into columns — the opposite direction. The source already has Q1/Q2/Q3 as columns, so pivoting would not help and would likely error.
Correct. Unpivot on Q1, Q2, Q3 converts each column into a row with Quarter (Attribute) and Sales (Value). 2 products × 3 quarters = 6 output rows.
Group By aggregates data within groups. It would produce one row per product with a total, not one row per product-quarter combination.

transformationPreview.label: Power Query Transformation

examObjective: Prepare the data > Resolve null values
commonTrap: Replacing null with 'Unknown' when Fill Down is the correct fix
question: The Category column appears as shown on the left. Every product row must show its correct category. Which Power Query transformation produces the result on the right?
choices: Fill Down the Category column
Remove rows where Category is null
Replace null values with 'Unknown'
Change the Category column data type to Whole Number
explanation: Fill Down propagates the last non-null value downward through each null cell. This recovers the correct category for each product row — the source used a merged-cell pattern where the category appears only on the first row of each group.
choiceExplanations: Correct. Fill Down propagates 'Sports' to Helmet and Gloves, and 'Office' to Chair — correctly reconstructing the grouped category structure.
Removing null rows would delete Helmet, Gloves, and Chair — valid product records that belong to their categories. This causes data loss.
Replacing with 'Unknown' discards the actual category. The category is not unknown — it is implied by the group above. Fill Down recovers it correctly.
Category is a text column. Changing its type to Whole Number would error on text values and does not address the null pattern.

transformationPreview.label: Category Column — Null Pattern

examObjective: Prepare the data > Merge queries
commonTrap: Expecting Merge to stack rows like Append
question: The two tables shown are combined using a Left Outer Merge on CustomerID. Which result correctly represents the output?
choices: An error — Merge requires both tables to have identical columns
2 rows — one row per unique customer, orders aggregated
5 rows — all Customers and Orders rows stacked vertically
3 rows — each Order row enriched with the customer Name
explanation: A Left Outer Merge joins Customers into Orders on CustomerID, adding the Name column to each Order row. There are 3 order rows, so the result has 3 rows — each with the matching customer name.
choiceExplanations: Merge is designed specifically for tables with different columns. The join key (CustomerID) must appear in both tables, but other columns are independent.
Merge does not aggregate. Summarizing orders per customer is a separate Group By step. Merge simply adds columns — it does not collapse rows.
Stacking rows vertically is Append, not Merge. Append requires identical column structures. Merge joins two tables horizontally on a shared key.
Correct. Left Outer Merge keeps all rows from Orders and adds matching columns from Customers. 3 order rows × matching CustomerID = 3 result rows with Name added.

examObjective: Model the data > RELATED and RELATEDTABLE
commonTrap: Using LOOKUPVALUE when RELATED is simpler and preferred
question: The model contains the two tables shown, connected by ProductID. You need to add a Category column to the Sales table. Which expression correctly creates this calculated column?
choices: RELATED(Products[Category])
VALUES(Products[Category])
CALCULATE(MAX(Products[Category]))
LOOKUPVALUE(Products[Category], Products[ProductID], Sales[ProductID])
explanation: RELATED(Products[Category]) uses the active ProductID relationship to retrieve the Category for each Sales row in row context. It is the preferred approach when a relationship exists — simpler and more efficient than LOOKUPVALUE.
choiceExplanations: Correct. RELATED(Products[Category]) uses the active relationship between Sales[ProductID] and Products[ProductID] to retrieve the category for each Sales row during column calculation.
VALUES(Products[Category]) returns a table with unique category values, not a single text value. Using it in a calculated column would cause a data type error.
CALCULATE(MAX(Products[Category])) in a calculated column has no row-level filter — it would return the same alphabetically-last category for every Sales row, ignoring ProductID.

LOOKUPVALUE works without a relationship and matches by column value. While valid here, RELATED is preferred when a relationship exists — it leverages the model's join rather than requiring explicit column matching.

subtopic: Design and implement a data model
examObjective: Model the data > Relationship cardinality
commonTrap: Assuming many-to-many when one side has unique keys
question: Examining the two tables shown, what is the correct cardinality for a relationship between Products and Sales on ProductID?
choices: One-to-one (1:1) — ProductID appears once in both tables
One-to-many (1:*) — ProductID is unique in Products but repeats in Sales
No relationship possible — the columns contain different data types
Many-to-many (*:*) — ProductID has duplicates in both tables
explanation: Products has unique ProductID values (P1, P2, P3 each appear once) — this is the 'one' side. Sales repeats the same ProductIDs across multiple rows — this is the 'many' side. The relationship is one-to-many (Products → Sales).
choiceExplanations: One-to-one requires unique ProductIDs in both tables. In Sales, P1 appears in rows 1 and 2 — it is not unique. This is not a 1:1 relationship.
Correct. Products[ProductID] has three unique values (P1, P2, P3) — the 'one' side. Sales[ProductID] repeats P1 twice — the 'many' side. This is a standard dimension-to-fact 1:* relationship.
Both columns contain text values in the same format (P1, P2, P3). Compatible types allow a relationship — there is no data type conflict here.
Many-to-many requires duplicates in both tables. Products clearly has unique IDs — it is the 'one' side of the relationship, not the 'many' side.

examObjective: Prepare the data > Group and aggregate rows
commonTrap: Thinking Group By retains individual row detail
question: A Group By step is applied to the source table, grouping by Region and summing Amount. Which output is produced?
choices: An error — Group By requires a date column
2 rows — one per unique Region with summed Amount values
5 rows sorted by Region — the rows are reordered but unchanged
3 rows — one per unique SalesRep
explanation: Group By on Region collapses all rows for each region into one: East = 100+300 = 400, West = 200+500+150 = 850. The result has exactly 2 rows — one per unique Region value.
choiceExplanations: Group By works on any column type. Date columns are relevant for time intelligence DAX functions, not Power Query Group By aggregations.
Correct. East has 2 rows (100+300=400), West has 3 rows (200+500+150=850). Group By produces 2 result rows.
Group By does not sort — it aggregates. The 5 source rows are collapsed into 2 grouped rows, not reordered.
SalesRep is not used as the group key — Region is. Group By on Region produces one row per unique Region, not one per SalesRep.

expectedOutput.label: After Group By Region, Sum Amount

examObjective: Prepare the data > Pivot data
commonTrap: Confusing Pivot with Unpivot direction
question: A Power Query transformation converts the normalized source table (Before) into the crosstab format (After). Which step achieves this?
choices: Transpose the entire table
Unpivot the Q1 and Q2 columns
Pivot the Quarter column using Sum as the aggregate
Merge the Q1 and Q2 rows per Region
explanation: Pivot on the Quarter column expands the unique Quarter values (Q1, Q2) into column headers, placing each Region's Amount in the correct cell. This converts the tall normalized format into the wide crosstab format.
choiceExplanations: Transpose flips all rows and columns globally. It would not produce a clean Region × Quarter crosstab — it would swap row and column roles unpredictably.
Unpivot goes the opposite direction — it converts columns into rows. The source is already in the narrow row format. Unpivoting would reverse the direction from what is needed.
Correct. Pivot(Quarter, Sum of Amount) creates Q1 and Q2 columns: East has Q1=100, Q2=150; West has Q1=200, Q2=250.
Merge combines two separate tables on a key. It does not restructure rows within a single table — this operation does not apply here.

transformationPreview.label: Power Query Transformation

subtopic: Design and implement a data model
examObjective: Model the data > Star schema design
commonTrap: Connecting dimension tables to each other instead of to the fact table
question: The four tables shown need to be connected in an optimal Power BI model. Which describes the correct star schema relationship structure?
choices: Date connects to Customers, which connects to Sales — a snowflake structure
All four tables connect to each other in a mesh pattern
Customers connects to Products, which connects to Sales — a chain structure
Sales is the fact table — Customers, Products, and Date connect directly to Sales
explanation: In a star schema, the central fact table (Sales) connects directly to each dimension table through one-to-many relationships. Dimension tables do not connect to each other — all filter propagation flows through the fact table.
choiceExplanations: Date → Customers → Sales is a chain, not a star. Date should connect directly to Sales through the date key in the fact table, not through an intermediary dimension.
A mesh pattern creates ambiguous filter paths and multiple active relationship routes. Power BI cannot resolve conflicting filter directions in a mesh — it would produce errors or incorrect results.

Chaining Customers → Products → Sales creates a snowflake schema. DAX must traverse multiple hops to filter, which adds complexity. Best practice is to connect each dimension directly to the fact table.

Correct. Sales is the fact table containing transactional data with foreign key columns. Customers, Products, and Date are dimension tables, each joining Sales with a 1:* relationship on their respective key.

subtopic: Design and implement a data model
examObjective: Model the data > Role-playing dimensions
commonTrap: Creating a second Date table instead of using USERELATIONSHIP
question: The Sales table has both OrderDate and ShipDate columns, both needing to join the Date dimension. Only one relationship can be active. The measure shown uses USERELATIONSHIP. What does this measure calculate?
choices: An error — USERELATIONSHIP cannot be used inside CALCULATE
Total sales filtered by OrderDate — the active relationship
Total sales across all dates regardless of date filters
Total sales filtered by ShipDate — the inactive relationship activated for this measure
explanation: USERELATIONSHIP(Sales[ShipDate], Date[Date]) inside CALCULATE activates the inactive ShipDate relationship for this specific measure. The OrderDate relationship remains the default active relationship for all other measures.
choiceExplanations: USERELATIONSHIP is specifically designed to be used inside CALCULATE. It is not valid outside of it, but within CALCULATE it is the standard approach for inactive relationships.
The OrderDate relationship is active by default — a plain SUM(Sales[Amount]) would use it. This measure explicitly overrides that by activating the ShipDate relationship instead.
USERELATIONSHIP does not remove filters — it changes which relationship path filters flow through. Date filters still apply; they now use the ShipDate column.
Correct. USERELATIONSHIP activates the inactive ShipDate→Date relationship for this CALCULATE expression only. Date slicers now filter Sales by ShipDate instead of OrderDate.
daxExpression:
Sales by Ship Date =
CALCULATE(
  SUM(Sales[Amount]),
  USERELATIONSHIP(Sales[ShipDate], Date[Date])
)

subtopic: Design and implement a data model
examObjective: Model the data > Common date table
commonTrap: Using only transaction dates instead of a complete continuous date table
question: A TOTALYTD measure is returning incorrect results. The Date table shown only includes dates where transactions occurred. What is the most likely cause of the problem?
choices: TOTALYTD requires a fiscal year end date parameter to work in January
The Sales table is missing a relationship to the Date table
The Date table has gaps — it must contain every calendar day with no missing dates
The Date table must be created using CALENDARAUTO() to be marked as a Date table
explanation: A Date table must have one continuous row per calendar day with no gaps. Skipping non-transaction dates (weekends, holidays) creates gaps that break time intelligence — TOTALYTD cannot determine correct period boundaries when dates are missing.
choiceExplanations: TOTALYTD works correctly with the default fiscal year end (December 31) and does not require an explicit parameter for January data. The end date parameter is optional and not the issue here.
A missing relationship would cause TOTALYTD to return BLANK for all rows, not incorrect values. If values are appearing but are wrong, the relationship likely exists.
Correct. The Date table must include every calendar day — not just transaction dates. Missing Jan 3, 4, 6, 7 means TOTALYTD cannot correctly accumulate the year-to-date total across those periods.
CALENDARAUTO() is one way to create a Date table, but any continuous date table marked as a Date table will work. The creation method is not the issue — the gaps are.

subtopic: Design and implement a data model
examObjective: Model the data > Many-to-many relationships
commonTrap: Using bidirectional filtering instead of a bridge table
question: Products and Promotions have a many-to-many relationship — each product can have multiple promotions and each promotion applies to multiple products. The three tables shown are available. Which design correctly resolves the many-to-many?
choices: Use CROSSFILTER() in every measure that needs promotion data
Set the Products-to-Promotions relationship to bidirectional filtering
Merge Promotions into the Products table as a text column
Use a bridge table (ProductPromotion) connecting Products and Promotions through two 1:* relationships
explanation: A bridge (junction) table resolves many-to-many into two one-to-many relationships: Products → ProductPromotion (1:*) and Promotions → ProductPromotion (1:*). This gives predictable filter behavior and avoids the double-counting issues that native M:M can produce.
choiceExplanations: CROSSFILTER() in DAX measures is a per-calculation workaround. A properly structured bridge table solves the problem at the model level, eliminating the need for repeated CROSSFILTER calls.
Bidirectional filtering allows filters to flow both ways but does not resolve the fundamental M:M structure. It can cause ambiguous filter paths and double-counting in measures.
Merging Promotions into Products as text loses relational integrity and prevents filtering by promotion attributes. This approach does not scale when promotions change.

Correct. The bridge table ProductPromotion creates two 1:* relationships: Products → ProductPromotion and Promotions → ProductPromotion. Filters flow cleanly through the bridge without double-counting.

examObjective: Prepare the data > Append queries
commonTrap: Using Merge when Append is needed for identical-structure tables
question: Two regional sales tables with identical column structures must be combined into one unified table as shown in the result. Which Power Query operation produces this output?
choices: Append queries
Duplicate the East table and manually add rows
Merge queries using a Left Outer Join on Product
Reference the East table and add a transformation step
explanation: Append stacks tables with identical column structures vertically — all rows from both tables become rows in the combined table. The result has 4 rows: 2 from East + 2 from West. Merge would join them horizontally, not stack them.
choiceExplanations: Correct. Append stacks the East and West tables vertically. All 4 rows (2 from each region) appear in the combined output with no structural change.
Manually adding rows is not a scalable Power Query pattern. It hard-codes data into the query and breaks when source data changes. Append is the correct dynamic approach.
Merge joins tables horizontally on a shared key — adding columns, not rows. Merging East and West on Product would add a second Amount column, not stack the rows.
Referencing the East table creates a query that inherits East's transformations but produces no automatic combination with West. You would still need an Append step.

question: A Sales table has Qty and UnitPrice columns but no Revenue column. A report needs total revenue across all transactions. Which DAX expression is correct?
choices: SUM(Sales[Qty]) * SUM(Sales[UnitPrice])
SUM(Sales[Revenue])
SUMX(Sales, Sales[Qty] * Sales[UnitPrice])
CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Qty] * Sales[UnitPrice]))
explanation: SUMX iterates each row, computing Qty × UnitPrice per row, then sums the results. SUM(Qty) * SUM(Price) multiplies grand totals rather than per-row values — this is mathematically wrong. SUM(Sales[Revenue]) would fail because Revenue does not exist as a column.
choiceExplanations: SUM(Qty) × SUM(UnitPrice) multiplies the grand totals of both columns, not per-row products. If rows have varying prices and quantities, the result is mathematically incorrect.
SUM(Sales[Revenue]) would fail immediately because no Revenue column exists in the table — you cannot SUM a column that has not been stored.
Correct. SUMX iterates each row, computing Qty × UnitPrice per row, then sums all per-row results.
SUM() requires a single column reference — it cannot accept an expression like Sales[Qty] * Sales[UnitPrice]. This is a syntax error in DAX.

question: A developer uses ALL(Sales[Region]) as a filter argument inside CALCULATE to remove the Region slicer filter. Which alternative function achieves the same result?
choices: FILTER(Sales, Sales[Region] = BLANK())
VALUES(Sales[Region])
REMOVEFILTERS(Sales[Region])
DISTINCT(Sales[Region])
explanation: REMOVEFILTERS(Sales[Region]) is functionally equivalent to ALL(Sales[Region]) when used as a filter argument inside CALCULATE — both remove the Region filter from the current context. REMOVEFILTERS is preferred because its name more clearly communicates the intent.
choiceExplanations: FILTER(Sales, Sales[Region] = BLANK()) returns rows where Region is blank — it does not remove the Region filter. It applies a new filter rather than removing the existing one.
VALUES(Sales[Region]) returns a table of distinct Region values currently in context — it does not remove any filter. It respects the filter rather than ignoring it.
Correct. REMOVEFILTERS(Sales[Region]) is functionally equivalent to ALL(Sales[Region]) inside CALCULATE — both remove the Region column filter.
DISTINCT(Sales[Region]) returns a table of unique Region values, similar to VALUES. It does not remove filters — it returns the filtered distinct values.
daxExpression:
-- ALL(Sales[Region]) removes filters on the Region column
Revenue All Regions =
    CALCULATE([Total Revenue], ALL(Sales[Region]))

-- Equivalent using REMOVEFILTERS:
Revenue All Regions =
    CALCULATE([Total Revenue], REMOVEFILTERS(Sales[Region]))

-- Both produce identical results.
-- REMOVEFILTERS is more explicit about intent.

question: A calculated column in the Sales fact table needs to retrieve the Product Category from the Products dimension table. The relationship is one-to-many from Products to Sales. Which function is correct?
choices: LOOKUPVALUE(Sales[ProductID], Products[ProductID])
RELATED(Products[Category])
VALUES(Products[Category])
RELATEDTABLE(Products[Category])
explanation: RELATED traverses from the many-side (Sales fact table) to the one-side (Products dimension). Each Sales row has exactly one matching Products row, so RELATED returns a single Category value. RELATEDTABLE goes the opposite direction and returns a table, not a scalar.
choiceExplanations: LOOKUPVALUE searches for matching values without using the model relationship. The syntax here is also wrong — LOOKUPVALUE takes result column, search column, and search value. Use RELATED when an active relationship already exists.
Correct. RELATED traverses from the many-side (Sales) to the one-side (Products) and returns the matching Category scalar value.

VALUES(Products[Category]) returns a table of distinct Category values in the current filter context — not a row-level column lookup from a related table. It cannot be stored in a calculated column row by row.

RELATEDTABLE returns all related rows as a TABLE — it traverses from the one-side to the many-side, the opposite direction from a Sales calculated column. You would get a table of products per sales row, not a single value.

question: A Power BI model has Qty and UnitPrice in the Sales table. A revenue total is needed that responds correctly to slicers and cross-filter interactions in reports. Should this be implemented as a measure or a calculated column?
choices: Measure — it evaluates dynamically in the current filter context and responds to slicers
Calculated column — DAX iterators only work on stored columns, not measures
Either approach produces identical results for report aggregations
Calculated column — it computes a value per row which SUMX can then aggregate
explanation: A measure evaluates dynamically within the current filter context and responds correctly to slicers, visuals, and cross-filters. A calculated column is computed once at refresh and stored row by row — it does not respond to filter context changes in reports. For aggregated reporting metrics, always use a measure.
choiceExplanations: Correct. A measure evaluates dynamically in the current filter context, responding to all slicer, visual, and cross-filter interactions at query time.

DAX iterators like SUMX can iterate any table expression — they do not require stored columns. A calculated column approach adds stored redundancy to the model unnecessarily without giving dynamic filter response.

The results differ significantly. A calculated column value is frozen at refresh; a measure recalculates dynamically on every visual interaction. For aggregated reporting metrics, they are not equivalent.

A calculated column does compute row-level values, but it is stored as fixed data at refresh time and does not respond to slicer or cross-filter context changes in reports. Aggregating it later still won't give you dynamic filter response.

tables.name: Measure vs Calculated Column for slicer-responsive revenue
rows: NO — stored at refresh, fixed per row
NO — card shows same total regardless of slicer

question: A developer writes the following measure: Sales Amount = CALCULATE(Sales[Amount], Sales[Region] = "East"). What is wrong with this expression?
choices: Nothing — this is valid DAX syntax
CALCULATE requires a scalar expression as its first argument, but Sales[Amount] is a column reference — not a scalar
CALCULATE does not support string comparison filters
The filter condition must use double quotes around column names
explanation: CALCULATE's first argument must be a scalar expression such as a measure or aggregation like SUM(Sales[Amount]). A bare column reference Sales[Amount] is not a scalar — it represents an entire column. The correct expression is CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), Sales[Region] = "East").
choiceExplanations: The expression is invalid. CALCULATE(Sales[Amount], ...) passes a column reference where a scalar expression is required — such as SUM(), AVERAGE(), or a measure reference.
Correct. CALCULATE's first argument must be a scalar expression such as SUM(Sales[Amount]). A bare column reference like Sales[Amount] is not scalar — it represents an entire column of values.
CALCULATE fully supports string comparison filter arguments like Sales[Region] = "East". The problem is not the string comparison — it is the column reference in the first argument position.
Column names do not need quotes in DAX. Values in string comparisons use double quotes, but table[column] references are written without any quotes. The filter argument syntax is not the issue here.
daxExpression:
-- WRONG: Sales[Amount] is a column reference, not a scalar
Sales Amount = CALCULATE(Sales[Amount], Sales[Region] = "East")  -- ❌

-- CALCULATE first argument MUST be a scalar expression (a measure or aggregation)
Sales Amount = CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), Sales[Region] = "East")  -- ✅
Sales Amount = CALCULATE([Total Revenue], Sales[Region] = "East")     -- ✅

question: A developer writes this DAX as a standalone measure: High Value = FILTER(Sales, Sales[Amount] > 500). What problem does this cause?
choices: FILTER requires a date column as its first argument
The measure returns a table instead of a scalar — DAX measures must return a single scalar value
FILTER is not allowed inside measure definitions
Sales[Amount] cannot be compared to a numeric literal
explanation: FILTER returns a TABLE of matching rows, not a scalar. A measure must return a single scalar value. To use this filter meaningfully, wrap it inside a function that accepts a table: CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), FILTER(Sales, Sales[Amount] > 500)) or COUNTROWS(FILTER(Sales, Sales[Amount] > 500)).
choiceExplanations: FILTER can work on any table — it does not require a date column. The first argument is any table expression; the second is a row-level Boolean condition. There is no restriction to date columns.
Correct. FILTER returns a TABLE of rows. A DAX measure must return a scalar value. Wrap FILTER in COUNTROWS() or use it inside CALCULATE to produce a scalar result.
FILTER is valid inside measure definitions. The issue is not where it appears but what it returns — a table. A measure must return a scalar value, not a table.
DAX can compare column values to numeric literals using standard comparison operators. Sales[Amount] > 500 is valid DAX syntax — that is not the source of the problem.
daxExpression:
-- WRONG: FILTER returns a table — measures must return a scalar
High Value = FILTER(Sales, Sales[Amount] > 500)  -- ❌ ERROR in a measure

-- CORRECT: wrap FILTER in an aggregation to get a scalar
High Value Count = COUNTROWS(FILTER(Sales, Sales[Amount] > 500))  -- ✅
High Value Total = SUMX(FILTER(Sales, Sales[Amount] > 500), Sales[Amount])  -- ✅

question: A Product Rank measure is defined as: Rank = RANKX(Products, SUM(Sales[Amount])). A matrix visual shows 8 products filtered by a category slicer. What is the maximum rank number visible?
choices: An error — RANKX requires ALL() as the first argument
1 — all products tie at rank 1 without ALL()
The product's rank among all products in the entire model
8 — ranks are calculated only against the 8 currently visible products
explanation: Without ALL(Products), RANKX evaluates the table argument within the current filter context — meaning it only considers the 8 visible products. Each product is ranked 1–8 relative to that visible set. To rank against all products regardless of slicers, use RANKX(ALL(Products), SUM(Sales[Amount])).
choiceExplanations: ALL() is not required syntax for RANKX. It is commonly used to expand the ranking scope to all items in the model, but RANKX works without it — it just ranks within the currently filtered set.
RANKX does not produce a tie of rank 1 for all items by default. Without ALL(), it ranks correctly within the visible set — the scope of ranking changes, not whether ranking works at all.
Without ALL(Products), RANKX only considers the rows visible in the current filter context — not the entire model. The rank shown is relative to visible products only, not the full product catalog.
Correct. Without ALL(), RANKX evaluates within the current filter context — ranking the 8 visible products from 1 to 8.
daxExpression:
Product Rank = RANKX(Products, SUM(Sales[Amount]))

-- WITHOUT ALL(), RANKX uses the products in the current filter context.
-- If the visual filters to 8 products, RANKX ranks those 8 — not all products.
-- Ranks 1–8 appear (not 1, 5, 12... against the full catalog).

expectedOutput.label: RANKX without ALL — relative ranks within the visual filter

subtopic: Create model calculations by using DAX
question: A Sales table has both OrderDate and ShipDate columns. Both are connected to DimDate, but only the OrderDate relationship is active. A measure must aggregate Sales filtered by ShipDate when the date slicer is used. What is the correct approach?
choices: Change the active relationship from OrderDate to ShipDate in the model
Use USERELATIONSHIP(Sales[ShipDate], DimDate[Date]) inside CALCULATE
Create a second DimDate table dedicated to ShipDate
Use RELATED(DimDate[Date]) to pull the date into Sales
explanation: USERELATIONSHIP temporarily activates an existing inactive relationship within the scope of a CALCULATE expression. This allows the ShipDate relationship to drive date filtering for this specific measure without changing the model's default active relationship.
daxExpression:
Shipped Sales =
CALCULATE(
  SUM(Sales[Amount]),
  USERELATIONSHIP(Sales[ShipDate], DimDate[Date])
)
choiceExplanations: Changing the active relationship would break all existing measures and reports that rely on OrderDate filtering. The inactive relationship exists precisely so that each can be used selectively without restructuring the model.
Correct. USERELATIONSHIP inside CALCULATE temporarily activates the inactive ShipDate relationship for this specific measure's evaluation without changing the model's default active relationship.

Creating a second DimDate table wastes model size, requires duplicate maintenance, and adds complexity every time you update the calendar. USERELATIONSHIP is the purpose-built solution that avoids duplicating the date table.
RELATED retrieves a value by traversing the active relationship — it does not activate an inactive relationship or affect how DAX propagates date filters through the model during calculation.

question:
A developer writes the following measure:

Sales Compare =
VAR CurrentSales = SUM(Sales[Amount])
VAR LastYear = CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(DimDate[Date]))
RETURN CurrentSales - LastYear

What filter context does VAR CurrentSales capture?
choices: An error — VAR cannot contain aggregation functions
The current filter context at the point the VAR line is executed — the period selected in the visual
The grand total — VAR ignores filter context
The prior year's filter context, because LastYear is declared after
explanation: Variables in DAX are evaluated at the point of their declaration, within the filter context that exists at that moment. VAR CurrentSales captures SUM(Sales[Amount]) in whatever filter context the measure is currently evaluated — the period selected by slicers and visuals.
choiceExplanations: VAR can contain any valid DAX expression including aggregation functions, measures, and CALCULATE expressions. There is no restriction on using aggregations inside VAR declarations.
Correct. VAR CurrentSales evaluates SUM(Sales[Amount]) in the filter context active at the time the VAR line executes — the current period selected by slicers and report visuals.
Variables do not ignore filter context. Each VAR captures the filter context exactly as it exists at the moment its line is evaluated — which is the currently active slicer and visual filter context.

Variables are evaluated in declaration order within the same filter context. The order of VAR declarations does not affect what filter context each one captures — each captures the same outer context independently.
daxExpression:
Sales Compare =
VAR CurrentSales = SUM(Sales[Amount])            -- captures CURRENT filter context
VAR LastYear    = CALCULATE(
                    SUM(Sales[Amount]),
                    SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date])
                  )
RETURN CurrentSales - LastYear

-- KEY: VAR captures the filter context at the moment the VAR line is evaluated.
-- CurrentSales = sum for the period shown in the visual (e.g., March 2024).
-- CALCULATE inside a VAR can still modify the context for that specific calculation.

expectedOutput.label: What each VAR captures
rows: March 2024 → shifted to March 2023 by SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR

question: Inside the expression SUMX(Sales, CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]))), what role does CALCULATE play?
choices: Nothing — CALCULATE is redundant inside an iterator and is ignored
It resets the filter context to the entire Sales table for every row
It creates a relationship between the row being iterated and the outer filter context
It performs context transition, converting the current row context into an equivalent filter context on the Sales table
explanation: When CALCULATE appears inside an iterator like SUMX, it performs context transition — it converts the current row context (the values of the row being evaluated) into an equivalent filter context applied to the full table. This is a key DAX behavior that enables complex row-level filtering within iterators.
choiceExplanations: CALCULATE inside an iterator is never ignored — it always performs context transition, which is a fundamental and intentional DAX behavior that enables complex row-level calculations.

CALCULATE inside an iterator does not reset to the entire Sales table. Context transition applies the current row as a filter — the filter context becomes more specific (filtered to that row), not unrestricted.

CALCULATE does not create relationships between rows or contexts. Context transition converts row context to filter context — it operates entirely within the DAX filter/evaluation mechanism, not the model relationship layer.

Correct. CALCULATE inside SUMX triggers context transition, converting the current row context into an equivalent filter context, allowing the inner SUM to evaluate correctly for each row being iterated.
daxExpression:
-- Context transition: CALCULATE inside SUMX converts row context → filter context
SUMX(Sales, CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount])))

-- Without CALCULATE: SUMX(Sales, Sales[Amount]) is fine (row context)
-- With CALCULATE wrapping: each iteration creates a filter matching the current row
-- Equivalent to: for each row, CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), Sales[OrderID] = current row)
-- This is "context transition" — row context becomes an equivalent filter context

question: Which DAX expression correctly returns the total sales for the same date range one year earlier than the current visual selection?
choices: CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), DATEADD(DimDate[Date], 1, YEAR))
CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), LASTDATE(DimDate[Date]) - 365)
CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), PREVIOUSYEAR(DimDate[Date]))
CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), DATEADD(DimDate[Date], -1, YEAR))
explanation: DATEADD with -1, YEAR shifts the current date selection back by exactly one year, preserving the same period offset. PREVIOUSYEAR returns the entire prior calendar year — not the same relative period. Subtracting 365 from LASTDATE is unreliable and ignores leap years.
daxExpression: Sales LY = CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), DATEADD(DimDate[Date], -1, YEAR))

choiceExplanations.0: DATEADD with +1 YEAR shifts the date context forward by one year, returning next year's equivalent period — the opposite of what is needed here.
choiceExplanations.1: Subtracting 365 from LASTDATE returns a single calculated date value, not a time-intelligence date table. It also ignores leap years and does not shift the full date range for the current selection.
choiceExplanations.2: PREVIOUSYEAR returns all dates of the entire previous calendar year (January 1 through December 31), not the same relative period shifted back one year.
choiceExplanations.3: Correct. DATEADD(DimDate[Date], -1, YEAR) shifts the current filter context's date range back by exactly one year, preserving the same period length and offset — the standard same-period-last-year pattern.

question: A measure uses SELECTEDVALUE(Products[Category], "All Categories"). No Category slicer exists on the report page. What does the measure return?
choices: The first Category value alphabetically
An error — SELECTEDVALUE requires a slicer to function
"All Categories" — the alternate result is returned when more than one value is visible
BLANK()
explanation: SELECTEDVALUE returns its second argument (the alternate result) when zero or more than one distinct value is visible for the specified column. With no slicer, all categories are visible simultaneously — multiple values are present — so the measure returns "All Categories". It never errors; the alternate result handles this case.

choiceExplanations.0: SELECTEDVALUE does not sort or pick alphabetically. It only returns a scalar when exactly one distinct value is in context; otherwise it returns the alternate result.
choiceExplanations.1: SELECTEDVALUE never throws an error. The second parameter (the alternate result) is specifically designed to handle the case when zero or more than one value is visible.
choiceExplanations.2: Correct. With no slicer, all Category values are visible simultaneously. Because more than one distinct value is present, SELECTEDVALUE returns its second argument — "All Categories".
choiceExplanations.3: SELECTEDVALUE returns BLANK() only when no second argument is provided and multiple values are visible. Here the second argument "All Categories" is explicitly supplied, so BLANK() is never returned.

daxExpression:
Label = SELECTEDVALUE(Products[Category], "All Categories")

-- SELECTEDVALUE returns the single selected value if exactly one category is filtered.
-- If zero or more than one category is visible → returns the alternate result.
-- When no Category slicer exists: all categories are visible → returns "All Categories"

question: A calculated column Category = RELATED(Products[Category]) is added to the Sales fact table. When is this column's values computed?
choices: When the report page is first opened by a user
Only when the column is used inside a DAX measure
During data refresh — the values are computed and stored in the model
Each time a visual queries the Sales table
explanation: Calculated columns are evaluated at data refresh time and stored row-by-row in the model's in-memory columnar store. This means they increase model size but allow the column to be used in relationships, slicers, row-level security filters, and other model-level features.

choiceExplanations.0: Calculated columns are not evaluated when the report page opens. They are already stored in the model by the time a user opens the report.
choiceExplanations.1: Calculated columns are computed and persisted during refresh regardless of whether any measure references them. They are not computed on demand at query time.
choiceExplanations.2: Correct. Calculated columns are evaluated row-by-row at data refresh time and their values are stored in the model's in-memory columnar store. This is why they increase model size but can be used in relationships, slicers, and RLS filters.
choiceExplanations.3: Each time a visual queries the table describes how measures behave (dynamic evaluation per query). Calculated columns are static — computed once at refresh and stored.

tables.name: When calculated column values are computed
rows: NO — stored value, fixed until refresh

question: A Sales table contains Qty and UnitPrice columns. You need the average revenue per transaction — where revenue is Qty × UnitPrice for each row. Which measure is correct?
choices: AVERAGE(Sales[UnitPrice]) * AVERAGE(Sales[Qty])
AVERAGEX(Sales, Sales[Qty] * Sales[UnitPrice])
AVERAGE(Sales[Qty] * Sales[UnitPrice])
DIVIDE(SUM(Sales[Qty] * Sales[UnitPrice]), COUNT(Sales[Qty]))
explanation: AVERAGEX iterates each row, computes Qty × UnitPrice per row, then averages all row results. AVERAGE() only works on a single existing column. Option D (average of averages) is mathematically wrong — it does not equal the average of the product. Option C syntax is invalid — SUM() cannot take an arithmetic expression.

choiceExplanations.0: Multiplying two separate AVERAGE calls does not give the average of the row-level product. For example, if one row is Qty=1, Price=100 and another is Qty=100, Price=1, the averages multiplied give 50.5×50.5 = 2550.25, but the correct average revenue is (100+100)/2 = 100.
choiceExplanations.1: Correct. AVERAGEX iterates each row in Sales, computes Qty × UnitPrice for that row, then averages all the row results — giving the true average per-transaction revenue.
choiceExplanations.2: AVERAGE() accepts only a single column reference, not an arithmetic expression. This syntax is invalid in DAX and will produce an error.
choiceExplanations.3: SUM() does not accept an arithmetic expression involving two columns. The expression inside SUM() must be a single column reference; this syntax is invalid in DAX.

question: A measure is defined as: East Sales = CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), Sales[Region] = "East"). A report slicer is currently set to Region = "West". What value does this measure return?
choices: Sales for West only — the slicer filter takes precedence over CALCULATE
BLANK() — conflicting filters on the same column return an empty result
Sales for both East and West combined
Sales for East only — CALCULATE's filter argument overrides the slicer's Region filter
explanation: By default, filter arguments inside CALCULATE replace any existing filter on the same column. The slicer's Region = West filter is overridden by CALCULATE's Region = East filter. The measure always returns East sales regardless of the slicer. To intersect the two filters instead of replacing, use KEEPFILTERS(Sales[Region] = "East").

choiceExplanations.0: CALCULATE's filter arguments override the existing filter context for the same column. The slicer's West filter is replaced by East, not combined with it.
choiceExplanations.1: Conflicting filters on the same column do not produce BLANK by default. CALCULATE replaces the existing filter, so one filter wins — in this case, CALCULATE's explicit filter argument.
