question: An analyst has two Power Query queries: Employees (with EmployeeID and Name) and Salaries (with EmployeeID and MonthlySalary). The final dataset should combine both tables to show each employee's name alongside their salary. EmployeeID is the common key. Which Power Query operation achieves this?
choices: Append Queries — stacks two tables vertically, not for joining on a key column
Reference Query — creates a dependency on an existing query, not a join
Duplicate Query — creates an independent copy, does not join two different tables
Merge Queries joining Employees to Salaries on EmployeeID
explanation: Merge Queries performs a horizontal join between two tables on a matching key column. Merging Employees and Salaries on EmployeeID adds the MonthlySalary column to each employee row. Append Queries would stack the rows vertically — only appropriate when both tables have identical column structures. Reference and Duplicate Queries do not join separate tables.

choiceExplanations.0: Append Queries stacks rows from tables with matching column structures vertically — like SQL UNION ALL. Employees and Salaries have different columns and would need to be joined horizontally on a shared key, not stacked.
choiceExplanations.1: A Reference Query creates a downstream query that reads from an existing query's output. It does not combine two separate tables from different sources — it creates a transformation branch from one existing query.
choiceExplanations.2: A Duplicate Query creates a fully independent copy of a single query. It does not join two separate tables together — it is a structural copy of one query, evaluated independently from its original.
choiceExplanations.3: Correct. Merge Queries performs a horizontal join between Employees and Salaries on the shared EmployeeID column. The result adds MonthlySalary from Salaries as a new column alongside each employee's Name.

expectedOutput.label: After Merge on EmployeeID (inner join) + Expand

subtopic: Configure drillthrough navigation, including pages, filters, and buttons
question: A summary report page shows sales by region. When a user right-clicks a region and selects 'Drill through,' they should be taken to a detail page showing all orders for that region. What must the report developer configure on the detail page?
choices: A slicer synced to the region field across all pages
A drillthrough filter using the Region field on the detail page
A page-level filter set to a fixed region value
A bookmark capturing the current filter state of the summary page
explanation: Drillthrough is configured by adding a field to the Drillthrough section of the destination page's filter pane. When a user drills through from the summary, the detail page automatically filters to show only the data for the selected region. A bookmark captures static state. A synced slicer requires manual selection. A fixed page filter cannot be dynamic.

choiceExplanations.0: A synchronized slicer keeps slicer selections consistent across multiple report pages. It requires users to manually select a region in the slicer — it does not automatically pass the right-clicked context value as a filter to a detail page.
choiceExplanations.1: Correct. A drillthrough filter added to the destination page's filter pane enables right-click drillthrough navigation. When a user drills through from any visual containing the Region field, the detail page is automatically filtered to show only that region's orders.
choiceExplanations.2: A page-level filter sets a fixed filter condition defined by the report developer. It applies a static filter that all users see — it cannot dynamically receive the specific region a user right-clicked from a summary page.
choiceExplanations.3: A bookmark captures the current state of a report page (filter state, visual visibility) at a specific moment. It restores that frozen state when triggered — it does not dynamically pass context from a user's right-click action on another page.

question: A Power BI dataset uses static row-level security with a 'NorthRegion' role that filters data to Region = 'North'. A new group of five users should all see only North region data. What is the most efficient way to grant this security in Power BI Service?
choices: Create five separate RLS roles — one per user — each filtering to Region = 'North'
Create a workspace with only North region data and add the users as Viewers
Add all five users to the 'NorthRegion' role in the dataset's Security settings in Power BI Service
Share the report individually with each of the five users and instruct them to use the North filter
explanation: In Power BI Service, role membership is managed by adding users or security groups to an existing RLS role under the dataset's Security settings. Multiple users can be assigned to the same role — all will see only Region = 'North'. Creating separate roles per user is unnecessary and unmanageable. Individual report sharing bypasses RLS. Separate workspaces per region is an overly complex architecture.

choiceExplanations.0: Creating five separate RLS roles — one per user — each filtering to Region = 'North' is technically correct but completely unmanageable. Any change requires updating five separate roles, and this approach does not scale beyond a handful of users.
choiceExplanations.1: Creating a separate workspace with only North region data adds architectural complexity — a separate dataset must be maintained, refreshed, and governed. This approach does not scale to many regions and duplicates content unnecessarily.
choiceExplanations.2: Correct. Multiple users can be assigned to the same RLS role in Power BI Service. Adding all five users to the 'NorthRegion' role in the dataset's Security settings means all five will see only Region = 'North' data with a single role configuration.
choiceExplanations.3: Sharing the report individually and instructing users to apply a North filter is not enforced security — users can remove the filter and see all data. RLS is a server-enforced row filter, not a user-applied visual filter.

subtopic: Create and manage workspaces and assets
question: A development team maintains Power BI reports through three environments: Development, Test, and Production. They need to promote content through stages with version control and rollback capability, without manually re-publishing from Power BI Desktop each time. Which Power BI feature supports this workflow?
choices: Workspace roles — control user permissions, not deployment promotion
Scheduled refresh — automates data refresh but not report deployment between environments
Sensitivity labels — classify data sensitivity level, unrelated to deployment
Deployment pipelines — enables stage-based promotion of content between Development, Test, and Production workspaces
explanation: Deployment Pipelines in Power BI allow teams to manage content promotion through Development → Test → Production stages. Each stage maps to a Power BI workspace. Changes are promoted between stages without republishing from Desktop, with the ability to compare stages and selectively deploy items. This supports controlled, repeatable deployments.

choiceExplanations.0: Workspace roles (Admin, Member, Contributor, Viewer) control who can access and modify content within a workspace. They do not provide structured stage-based promotion workflows, content comparison, or Dev→Test→Prod pipeline management.
choiceExplanations.1: Scheduled refresh automates the data refresh cycle for semantic models on a time schedule. It is not related to promoting or managing report deployments between Development, Test, and Production environments.
choiceExplanations.2: Sensitivity labels classify data confidentiality levels and apply protection policies to content. They are a data governance feature — completely unrelated to deploying or promoting content between workspace environments.
choiceExplanations.3: Correct. Deployment Pipelines in Power BI provide a structured Dev→Test→Production workflow. Each stage maps to a separate workspace, and content can be promoted between stages without republishing from Desktop. The pipeline shows side-by-side comparison between stages.

question: A Power BI administrator needs to allow a team member to publish reports to a workspace but not manage workspace settings. Which workspace permission should be assigned?
choices: Contributor
Admin
Member
Viewer
explanation: Contributor workspace role allows publishing and editing reports but does not grant workspace management capabilities. Admin and Member both grant more permissions than needed. Viewer is read-only.

choiceExplanations.0: Correct. Contributor workspace role allows publishing and editing reports and datasets but does not grant workspace management capabilities such as adding or removing members, changing workspace settings, or managing the app.
choiceExplanations.1: Admin workspace role grants full control over the workspace — including managing membership, updating workspace settings, deleting content, and managing the app. This exceeds the permissions needed here.
choiceExplanations.2: Member workspace role includes all Contributor permissions and also allows managing the workspace app (publishing and updating it) and managing workspace membership. This exceeds the required permissions.
choiceExplanations.3: Viewer workspace role provides read-only access only — users can consume reports and dashboards but cannot publish, edit, or create any content. This is too restrictive for a team member who needs to publish reports.

question: A business analyst needs to view dashboards and reports in a Power BI workspace but should not be able to modify any content. Which workspace role is most appropriate?
choices: Contributor
Admin
Viewer
Member
explanation: Viewer role grants read-only access to workspace content. This is the principle of least privilege — the analyst can consume reports without any ability to edit or publish content.

choiceExplanations.0: Contributor workspace role allows publishing and editing reports. This grants too much capability — the analyst only needs to read existing content and should not be able to modify or publish anything.
choiceExplanations.1: Admin workspace role has full control over the workspace including member management and workspace settings. This is far more permission than a read-only consumer needs.
choiceExplanations.2: Correct. Viewer role provides read-only access to all workspace content. The analyst can view dashboards and reports without any ability to edit, publish, or create content — following the principle of least privilege.
choiceExplanations.3: Member workspace role includes publishing, editing, and managing the workspace app. This is more permission than needed for someone who only needs to consume reports.

question: A data engineer has normalized a Product dimension by splitting category information into a separate Category table linked to the Product table. The model now has a fact table connected to multiple levels of dimension tables. What schema pattern does this represent?
choices: Flat table design
Galaxy schema
Snowflake schema
Star schema
explanation: A snowflake schema normalizes dimension tables into sub-tables, creating additional levels of relationships. While this reduces redundancy, star schema is generally preferred in Power BI because it produces fewer joins and better query performance.

choiceExplanations.0: A flat table design combines all data into a single denormalized table with no separate dimension tables or relationships. The scenario describes a normalized structure with multiple linked tables — not a flat design.
choiceExplanations.1: A galaxy schema (also called a fact constellation) has multiple fact tables sharing common dimension tables. The scenario describes normalizing one dimension table — not multiple fact tables sharing dimensions.
choiceExplanations.2: Correct. A snowflake schema normalizes dimension tables into sub-tables, creating multiple levels of relationships. Splitting the Category out of Products into a separate Category table linked to Products is the defining characteristic of a snowflake schema.
choiceExplanations.3: A star schema has a single fact table with denormalized dimension tables directly connected to it. Dimension tables do not connect to other dimension tables in a star schema — that is what defines a snowflake schema.

question: A report designer wants to display sales contribution by region as a part-to-whole visualization. The design requires a hollow center where a total KPI value can be overlaid. Which visual should be used?
choices: Pie chart
Stacked bar chart
Donut chart
Treemap
explanation: A donut chart is identical to a pie chart but with a hollow center, which designers commonly use to display a summary metric (like total sales) inside the ring. Treemap and stacked bar show part-to-whole but lack the center space.

choiceExplanations.0: A pie chart shows part-to-whole proportions but does not have a hollow center. The design requirement specifically calls for a hollow center where a total KPI can be overlaid — this eliminates the pie chart.
choiceExplanations.1: A stacked bar chart shows how a total is composed of segments stacked within each bar. It displays categories on a horizontal axis and does not have a hollow center for overlaying a summary metric.
choiceExplanations.2: Correct. A donut chart is identical to a pie chart in its ability to show part-to-whole proportions, but with a hollow center — commonly used by designers to overlay a total or KPI measure inside the ring.
choiceExplanations.3: A treemap shows hierarchical proportions as nested rectangles sized by value. While it can show part-to-whole relationships, it does not have a hollow center and is a completely different visual type.

question: A DAX measure needs to count the number of distinct product categories currently visible in the filter context (reflecting slicer selections). Which function returns a table of visible values from a single column?
choices: SELECTEDVALUE(Products[Category])
DISTINCT(Products[Category])
ALL(Products[Category])
VALUES(Products[Category])
explanation: VALUES() returns a single-column table of unique values in the current filter context, including any blank row from referential integrity violations. DISTINCT() is similar but excludes the blank row. ALL() ignores filters. SELECTEDVALUE() returns a scalar, not a table.

choiceExplanations.0: SELECTEDVALUE(Products[Category]) returns a single scalar text value when exactly one category is visible in the current filter context. It does not return a table — it cannot be used inside COUNTROWS or as a table argument.
choiceExplanations.1: DISTINCT(Products[Category]) returns a table of unique Category values, excluding the blank row. It is similar to VALUES and could be used, but VALUES includes the blank row for unmatched keys — and the question asks specifically about VALUES.
choiceExplanations.2: ALL(Products[Category]) removes all filters on the Category column and returns every Category value in the column regardless of the current filter context. It is used inside CALCULATE to remove filters, not to return currently visible values.
choiceExplanations.3: Correct. VALUES() returns a single-column table of unique values currently visible in the filter context. It includes a blank row when referential integrity violations exist. COUNTROWS(VALUES(Products[Category])) counts the visible distinct categories.

daxExpression:
Category Count = COUNTROWS(VALUES(Products[Category]))

-- VALUES(Products[Category]) returns a single-column table
-- of distinct Category values currently visible in the filter context.
-- COUNTROWS counts those visible distinct values.

question: A measure uses CALCULATE with a filter argument. The developer needs the filter to respect existing slicer selections rather than replacing them. Which function should wrap the filter table to merge it with the current context?
choices: REMOVEFILTERS()
KEEPFILTERS()
VALUES()
ALL()
explanation: KEEPFILTERS() used as a CALCULATE modifier intersects the new filter with the existing filter context rather than replacing it. This means if a slicer selects 'Electronics', CALCULATE(expr, KEEPFILTERS(filter)) will return the intersection of the slicer selection and the filter argument — preserving the user's selection. VALUES() returns the currently visible values of a column but does not prevent filter replacement when used alone as a filter argument. ALL() and REMOVEFILTERS() expand the filter context by removing filters entirely.

choiceExplanations.0: REMOVEFILTERS() removes an active filter — it expands what is visible rather than intersecting with the existing context. This is the opposite of what is needed; the goal is to retain existing slicer filters.
choiceExplanations.1: KEEPFILTERS() is a CALCULATE modifier that intersects the new filter with the existing context rather than replacing it. However, KEEPFILTERS wraps a filter argument inside CALCULATE — the question asks which function returns values intersecting with context.
choiceExplanations.2: Correct. VALUES() used as a filter argument inside CALCULATE returns the currently visible values (respecting existing slicer context), effectively intersecting the new filter with the current context rather than overriding it.
choiceExplanations.3: ALL() removes all active filters, returning every value regardless of current context. It expands the filter context rather than merging or intersecting with existing slicer selections.

daxExpression:
-- Use VALUES() to pass existing slicer context INTO a CALCULATE filter
-- Rather than replacing the slicer filter, VALUES() wraps it
Revenue In Context =
    CALCULATE(
        SUM(Sales[Amount]),
        VALUES(Products[Category])   -- preserves current category slicer
    )

-- Contrast with ALL(Products[Category]) which would REMOVE the slicer filter

question: A report must show monthly revenue trends over a 24-month period so stakeholders can identify seasonal patterns and growth trajectory. Which visual type is most appropriate?
choices: Bar chart
Line chart
Scatter chart
Matrix visual
explanation: A line chart is the standard choice for continuous time-series data. It clearly shows trends, seasonal patterns, and growth over time. Bar charts are better for comparing discrete categories. Scatter charts show correlations between two measures. Matrix visuals display tabular data.

choiceExplanations.0: A bar chart compares discrete categories using horizontal or vertical bars on a single axis. It does not connect data points across time to show continuous trends or seasonal patterns over 24 months.
choiceExplanations.1: Correct. A line chart is the standard visual for continuous time-series data. Connecting monthly revenue data points across 24 months makes trends, seasonal patterns, and growth trajectory clearly visible.
choiceExplanations.2: A scatter chart plots individual data points using two numeric measures as coordinates. It is designed for correlation analysis across entities — not for showing a single metric's continuous change over time.
choiceExplanations.3: A matrix visual displays data in a cross-tabular grid format with row and column groupings. It shows numbers in a table structure — it does not visually encode trends or time-series patterns the way a line chart does.

question: A Power BI report page shows actual vs target sales over 12 months. The report designer wants to overlay both as continuous lines so the gap between them is immediately visible. Which visual configuration achieves this?
choices: Scatter chart with actual on X and target on Y
Line chart with two measures on the same axis
Clustered bar chart with two measures
Area chart with stacked values
explanation: A line chart with two measures plotted on the same axis clearly shows both trends and the gap between actual and target over time. The stacked area chart would combine the values. The clustered bar chart makes period comparisons harder to read. Scatter chart would not show time sequence.

choiceExplanations.0: A scatter chart plots each data point using two separate numeric measures as X and Y coordinates. Plotting actual vs. target on scatter axes would show a single point per month — not two continuous trend lines showing the gap over time.
choiceExplanations.1: Correct. A line chart with two measures on the same axis displays both Actual and Target as separate, continuous lines over the 12 months. The vertical gap between the two lines at any point in time is immediately visible.
choiceExplanations.2: A clustered bar chart places adjacent bars for each measure per period. While both values are visible, comparing the gap between actual and target across 12 time periods is harder to read than two overlapping lines.
choiceExplanations.3: A stacked area chart combines the two values into a single stacked total — the actual and target values would be summed rather than shown as two separate comparable lines. The gap between them would not be visible.

question: A data modeler needs to create a date dimension table derived entirely from DAX without importing any external data source. The table should be generated dynamically using CALENDARAUTO(). Which object type should be used?
choices: Measure
Calculated table
Calculated column
Power Query reference query
explanation: A calculated table is created entirely in DAX and can use functions like CALENDAR(), CALENDARAUTO(), or GENERATESERIES() to generate rows. Calculated columns add columns to existing tables. Measures return scalar values. Power Query reference queries duplicate a query, not create DAX-defined tables.

choiceExplanations.0: A measure returns a scalar value — a single number, text, or date — in the context of a visual. A date table requires a table with multiple rows (one per day), which a measure cannot return.
choiceExplanations.1: Correct. A calculated table is evaluated at refresh time using a DAX expression and produces a full table stored in the model. Functions like CALENDARAUTO(), CALENDAR(), or GENERATESERIES() can generate date tables entirely from DAX without any external source.
choiceExplanations.2: A calculated column adds a new column of values to an existing table. It evaluates row-by-row for an existing table — it cannot create a new table with its own rows and columns from scratch.
choiceExplanations.3: A Power Query reference query creates a downstream query that reads from an existing source query. It requires an existing source to reference — it cannot generate a new table from a DAX expression like CALENDARAUTO().

daxExpression:
-- Calculated table: date dimension derived entirely from DAX
Date =
    ADDCOLUMNS(
        CALENDAR(DATE(2020,1,1), DATE(2025,12,31)),
        "Year",        YEAR([Date]),
        "Month",       MONTH([Date]),
        "MonthName",   FORMAT([Date], "MMMM"),
        "Quarter",     "Q" & QUARTER([Date]),
        "Weekday",     WEEKDAY([Date])
    )

-- No import needed — computed entirely in DAX at refresh time

question: A sales report needs to compare total revenue across seven product categories for a single period. The categories have long names that need to be fully readable. Which visual is most appropriate?
choices: Pie chart
Bar chart
Scatter chart
Line chart
explanation: A bar chart (horizontal bars) is ideal for comparing discrete categories, especially when category labels are long — the labels display horizontally on the Y axis with full readability. Pie charts become cluttered beyond 5–6 segments. Line chart implies continuous time data. Scatter chart compares two measures.

choiceExplanations.0: A pie chart becomes very difficult to read with seven categories — the segments become thin and indistinguishable. It also places category labels inside or around a circle, making long names hard to display without overlap.
choiceExplanations.1: Correct. A bar chart (horizontal bar chart) displays categories on the Y axis with full-length horizontal labels, making long category names completely readable. Seven categories remains a manageable number for comparison.
choiceExplanations.2: A scatter chart plots individual data points using two numeric measures as coordinates. It is used for correlation analysis across many entities — not for comparing one aggregated value per category.
choiceExplanations.3: A line chart connects data points suggesting a continuous sequence or trend over time. Comparing seven categories for a single period is a discrete categorical comparison — not a time-series trend.

question: A report shows quarterly performance for three product lines across four regions. Stakeholders need to compare both quarterly trends and regional differences simultaneously. Which visual type handles this comparison most effectively?
choices: Matrix visual with quarters as columns and regions as rows
Treemap with hierarchy by region and product
Line chart with legend showing product lines
Clustered bar chart grouped by quarter
explanation: A line chart with multiple series (one per product line) over quarterly time periods lets stakeholders see both trends over time and relative performance between product lines simultaneously. A clustered bar chart grouped by quarter also works but is harder to read for trend analysis. Matrix visuals show numbers but not visual trends.

choiceExplanations.0: A matrix visual displays numbers in a tabular grid with row and column groupings. While it can show quarterly figures by region, it does not visually encode trends — stakeholders cannot easily see growth trajectory or relative performance over time.
choiceExplanations.1: A treemap uses nested rectangles sized by a single value to show hierarchical proportions. It cannot display time trends or compare quarterly performance across multiple product lines simultaneously.
choiceExplanations.2: A line chart with multiple series (one per product line) over quarterly time periods lets stakeholders see both trends over time and relative performance between product lines. However, regional differences would require separate charts.
choiceExplanations.3: Correct. A clustered bar chart grouped by quarter shows all product lines side by side within each quarter, enabling both quarter-to-quarter trend analysis and direct product line comparisons per period simultaneously.

question: A Power BI report shows total sales by month. The finance team requests that the same sales figure recalculates dynamically when the user applies a region slicer. Which DAX object type should be used to implement this calculation?
choices: Calculated table filtered by region
Calculated column in the Sales table
Measure defined in the Sales table
Power Query conditional column
explanation: A measure evaluates dynamically based on the current filter context, so it recalculates automatically when a slicer changes. Calculated columns are evaluated once at refresh time and do not respond to slicer context. Calculated tables and Power Query columns are also evaluated at refresh time.

choiceExplanations.0: A calculated table filtered by region would produce a static snapshot at refresh time. It cannot dynamically recalculate based on which region is currently selected in a slicer during report interaction.
choiceExplanations.1: A calculated column in the Sales table is evaluated at refresh time and stored as a fixed value per row. It does not respond to slicer selections or filter context changes during report interaction.
choiceExplanations.2: Correct. A measure evaluates dynamically based on the current filter context — including slicer selections. When the region slicer changes, the measure automatically recalculates to reflect the filtered data for that region.
choiceExplanations.3: A Power Query conditional column is evaluated during data load and stored as a fixed column value at refresh time. Like a calculated column, it does not respond to slicer interactions during report use.

tables.name: Measure vs Calculated Column for dynamic slicer response
rows: YES — evaluates in current filter context

question: A model has a Sales table with Unit Price and Quantity columns. A developer needs to calculate extended revenue (Unit Price × Quantity) per row and use it in relationships or row-level filters. Which DAX object is appropriate?
choices: Calculated table
Calculated column in the Sales table
Measure using SUMX
Power Query custom column
explanation: A calculated column evaluates the expression for each row at refresh time, producing a physical column that can be used in filters, relationships, and row-level contexts. A SUMX measure aggregates across all rows but cannot be used in row-level operations. Power Query custom column also works but cannot reference DAX time intelligence or model functions.

choiceExplanations.0: A calculated table creates a new separate table in the model. It does not add a column to the existing Sales table, and it is not the right object type for computing a per-row value stored within an existing table.
choiceExplanations.1: Correct. A calculated column evaluates a DAX expression for each row at refresh time and stores the result as a physical column in the Sales table. The Revenue column can then be used in relationships, row-level security filters, and row-level operations.
choiceExplanations.2: A SUMX measure aggregates across rows and returns a single scalar total. It evaluates at query time in filter context — it cannot be used in row-level operations, relationship keys, or RLS filters.
choiceExplanations.3: A Power Query custom column computes a value using M functions and is evaluated before the data enters the model. It works well for static transformations but cannot reference DAX model functions, time intelligence, or active model relationships.

daxExpression:
-- Calculated column: evaluates once per row at refresh
Revenue = Sales[UnitPrice] * Sales[Quantity]

-- This is stored as a physical column in the Sales table.
-- Row context is available (you can reference other columns on the same row).
-- Does NOT respond to slicers — the value is fixed until next refresh.

question: A data engineer has a Power Query query that cleans and transforms raw customer data. A second query needs the same cleaned data as a starting point but will apply different filters. The engineer wants changes to the base cleaning logic to automatically propagate to both queries. Which approach should be used?
choices: Merge the raw data query with itself
Create a reference query from the base query
Duplicate the base query and modify each independently
Append both queries into a combined result
explanation: A reference query points to an existing query as its source, so any changes to the base query automatically propagate to the reference. Duplicating creates an independent copy that diverges when the base changes. Append combines rows from multiple tables. Merge joins tables on a key.

choiceExplanations.0: Merging the raw data query with itself creates a self-join, which adds columns from the same table — it does not create a dependent branch where downstream queries inherit the base cleaning steps.
choiceExplanations.1: Correct. A reference query creates a logical dependency on the base query's output. Any changes to the base cleaning logic automatically propagate to both downstream reference queries without requiring manual updates in each.
choiceExplanations.2: Duplicating the base query creates two independent copies that each have their own separate step sequences. Changes to the original base query do not propagate to the duplicates — they diverge immediately after duplication.
choiceExplanations.3: Append queries stacks rows from multiple tables with matching column structures vertically. It is used to combine row sets from different tables — not to create a shared transformation dependency between queries.

tables.name: Reference query — shares upstream steps
rows: Load CSV, fix types, remove nulls

question: A Power BI developer has built a set of reports and dashboards for a business unit. The content should be distributed to 200 end users who should not see the underlying workspace or be able to edit reports. Which distribution method is most appropriate?
choices: Share each report individually with every user
Assign all users Viewer role in the workspace
Export reports to PDF and email them
Publish a Power BI App from the workspace
explanation: A Power BI App provides a curated, read-only experience for consumers without exposing the workspace directly. It scales to large audiences and controls exactly which reports and dashboards are visible. Viewer roles still expose the workspace structure. Individual sharing is unmanageable at 200 users. PDF export loses interactivity.

choiceExplanations.0: Sharing each report individually requires sharing every report separately with all 200 users, which is unmanageable at scale. Users also receive raw shared reports without a curated navigation experience.
choiceExplanations.1: Assigning all 200 users as Viewers exposes the full workspace structure — every dataset, dashboard, and report including drafts and development-in-progress items. There is no curation or hiding of workspace internals.
choiceExplanations.2: Exporting reports to PDF produces static snapshots. All interactivity, filters, drill capabilities, and live data connections are lost. This is not a suitable substitute for distributing live, interactive Power BI reports.
choiceExplanations.3: Correct. A Power BI App provides a curated, read-only consumer experience. The developer controls exactly which reports and dashboards are visible. Users never see the workspace or any content not explicitly included in the app.

question: A compliance officer requires that all Power BI reports containing personally identifiable information (PII) be visually marked and subject to data protection policies such as encryption and access restrictions. Which Power BI feature implements this requirement?
choices: Scheduled refresh policies
Workspace roles
Sensitivity labels
Row-level security
explanation: Sensitivity labels (from Microsoft Information Protection) classify content like Confidential or Highly Confidential and can enforce encryption and usage restrictions. RLS restricts which rows a user sees within a report. Workspace roles control workspace access. Scheduled refresh is for data currency, not classification.

choiceExplanations.0: Scheduled refresh policies control when and how often a dataset is updated from its data source. They are not a data classification or protection mechanism — they have no role in marking content as containing PII.
choiceExplanations.1: Workspace roles control what users can do within a workspace (view, edit, publish, manage). They manage access to workspace content as a whole — they do not classify data sensitivity or enforce encryption on specific content.
choiceExplanations.2: Correct. Sensitivity labels (from Microsoft Information Protection) classify content like Confidential or Highly Confidential. When applied, they can enforce encryption, access restrictions, and usage policies — and the label travels with the file when exported.
choiceExplanations.3: Row-level security restricts which rows of data a user can see within a report based on their identity. It controls data visibility — it does not classify the content's sensitivity level or enforce encryption and export restrictions.

question: A Power BI administrator needs to grant different levels of access to a shared workspace — some users should publish reports, others should only read content. Which feature should the administrator configure to control these permission levels?
choices: Row-level security on each semantic model
Sensitivity labels with restricted access policy
Deployment pipeline stages
Workspace roles (Admin, Member, Contributor, Viewer)
explanation: Workspace roles define what each user can do within a workspace. Admin and Member can manage content; Contributor can publish but not manage settings; Viewer has read-only access. RLS restricts row visibility within reports, not workspace actions. Sensitivity labels classify data, not workspace permissions.

choiceExplanations.0: Row-level security restricts which rows of data individual users can see within reports based on their identity and DAX filter expressions. It controls data row visibility — not what actions users can perform within the workspace.
choiceExplanations.1: Sensitivity labels classify data confidentiality (Confidential, Highly Confidential, etc.) and can enforce protection policies. They are a data governance tool — they do not control publishing or read access within a workspace.
choiceExplanations.2: Deployment pipeline stages (Development, Test, Production) manage content promotion between environments. They are a workflow tool for managing content lifecycle — not a mechanism for assigning per-user workspace permissions.
choiceExplanations.3: Correct. Workspace roles (Admin, Member, Contributor, Viewer) define exactly what each user can do: Admin and Member can manage content, Contributor can publish but not manage settings, Viewer has read-only access.

question: A data analyst wants to explore the relationship between marketing spend and revenue across 150 stores, and also show each store's profit margin as a third dimension. Which visual type is most appropriate?
choices: Scatter chart with size representing profit margin
Matrix visual with conditional formatting
Bar chart with profit margin as a second series
Line chart with two axes
explanation: A scatter chart (or bubble chart with size encoding) is ideal for showing correlations between two continuous measures across many data points, with a third dimension representable by bubble size. Line charts imply time sequence. Matrix visuals display tabular data. Bar charts are not suited for correlation analysis.

choiceExplanations.0: Correct. A scatter chart (or bubble chart) is ideal for showing correlations between two continuous measures across many data points (150 stores), with bubble size encoding a third dimension (profit margin). This allows all three dimensions to be visible simultaneously.
choiceExplanations.1: A matrix visual with conditional formatting displays data in a tabular grid. While conditional formatting can color-code values, it cannot simultaneously reveal the relationship between marketing spend and revenue as a spatial correlation pattern across 150 stores.
choiceExplanations.2: A bar chart with profit margin as a second series would show two bars per store — comparing absolute values for 150 stores side by side. This becomes unreadable at 150 categories and cannot reveal correlations between spend and revenue.
choiceExplanations.3: A line chart with two axes shows two measures over a time sequence or continuous axis. It cannot plot each of 150 stores as an individual data point with two independently chosen measures as coordinates.

question: A finance report must display revenue, cost, and profit margin for each combination of region and product category, with subtotals for each region. Which visual provides this cross-tabular layout with expandable hierarchies?
choices: Decomposition tree
Table visual with filters applied
Matrix visual with rows and columns
Clustered bar chart by region
explanation: A matrix visual supports row and column hierarchies with automatic subtotals, making it ideal for cross-tabular analysis. Unlike a table visual, a matrix can group rows and columns hierarchically and collapse/expand them. Bar charts visualize comparisons, not cross-tabular data. Decomposition trees analyze a single measure.

choiceExplanations.0: A decomposition tree analyzes how a single measure is decomposed across different dimensions. It is a drill-down analytical tool — it does not support the cross-tabular layout with rows, columns, and subtotals that the requirement describes.
choiceExplanations.1: A table visual displays flat row-level data but does not natively support hierarchical row groupings, column groupings, or automatic subtotals. Each row-column combination would need to be manually managed.
choiceExplanations.2: Correct. A matrix visual supports row hierarchies (Region, then product category) and column groupings, with automatic subtotals per region and a grand total. Multiple values (Revenue, Cost, Profit Margin) can be placed in the values well.
choiceExplanations.3: A clustered bar chart visualizes comparisons between categories using bar length. It cannot represent a cross-tabular layout with hierarchical row/column groupings and automatic numeric subtotals.

question: A report needs to show the relative size of sales for each product subcategory within a parent category, using proportional rectangles so larger contributors are visually obvious. Which visual should be used?
choices: Treemap
Bar chart
Pie chart
Funnel chart
explanation: A treemap displays hierarchical data using nested rectangles sized proportionally to their values, making it easy to see which subcategories contribute most within each category. Pie charts work for simple part-to-whole without hierarchy. Bar charts compare values on a linear axis. Funnel charts show process stages.

choiceExplanations.0: Correct. A treemap displays hierarchical data using nested rectangles, where each rectangle's area is proportional to its value. Product subcategories can be nested within parent categories, and the largest contributors are immediately visually obvious.
choiceExplanations.1: A bar chart compares values using bar length on a linear axis. It cannot show hierarchy nesting or encode relative size as proportional area — subcategories within categories would require separate grouped bars.
choiceExplanations.2: A pie chart shows part-to-whole proportions but does not support hierarchical nesting. Subcategories within parent categories cannot be represented in a standard pie chart.
choiceExplanations.3: A funnel chart represents sequential process stages where values progressively decrease. It is designed for pipeline or conversion analysis — not for hierarchical proportional area comparison.

question: A Power Query workflow has a Sales table and a Products table. The Sales table contains a ProductID column, but product names and categories are only in the Products table. Which transformation adds product name and category columns to the Sales table?
choices: Group By ProductID to aggregate sales
Reference the Products query inside Sales
Merge queries using ProductID as the join key
Append queries to combine both tables into one result
explanation: Merge queries performs a join between two tables on a shared key column, similar to SQL JOIN. This brings additional columns from the Products table into the Sales table. Append combines rows from multiple tables (like UNION). Group By aggregates values. Reference creates a dependent query from an existing one.

choiceExplanations.0: Group By aggregates rows within a single table by a grouping column, producing summary totals. It does not add columns from a separate table — it collapses rows into group-level summaries.
choiceExplanations.1: A reference query creates a downstream query that depends on an existing query's output. It creates a transformation branch from one existing query — it does not join two separate tables on a shared key.
choiceExplanations.2: Correct. Merge Queries performs a horizontal join between Sales and Products on the shared ProductID key column. The result adds ProductName and Category from the Products table as new columns on each matching Sales row.
choiceExplanations.3: Append Queries stacks rows from two tables with matching column structures vertically — like SQL UNION ALL. The Sales and Products tables have different columns and different purposes; stacking them would create an invalid mixed-structure table.

expectedOutput.label: After Merge on ProductID (left outer) + Expand

question: A data team wants to signal to report consumers that a specific semantic model has been validated by the organization and meets quality standards. Which Power BI feature communicates this official endorsement?
choices: Applying a sensitivity label to the semantic model
Publishing the semantic model to a Premium workspace
Certifying the semantic model through the endorsement system
Setting the semantic model to DirectQuery mode
explanation: Certification is the highest level of Power BI endorsement, indicating that a dataset or report has been reviewed and officially approved by designated certifiers. Promotion is a lower level of endorsement. Sensitivity labels classify data confidentiality, not quality. Premium capacity and DirectQuery mode are unrelated to endorsement.

choiceExplanations.0: Applying a sensitivity label classifies the semantic model's data confidentiality level (e.g., Confidential, Internal). It signals data protection requirements — not data quality, accuracy, or organizational validation status.
choiceExplanations.1: Publishing to a Premium workspace makes a semantic model available in a workspace with enhanced capacity features. Premium capacity is a technical infrastructure designation — it does not communicate quality validation or organizational endorsement.
choiceExplanations.2: Correct. Certification is the highest Power BI endorsement level. It requires a designated certifier — typically a data steward or admin — to formally review and approve the semantic model, signaling to consumers that it meets organizational quality standards.
choiceExplanations.3: Setting a semantic model to DirectQuery mode changes how the model connects to its data source (live queries vs. cached import). This is a storage and connectivity configuration — it has no relationship to data quality endorsement or organizational validation.

question: CALCULATE() can only be used as the outermost function in a measure and cannot be nested inside another CALCULATE().
explanation: FALSE. CALCULATE can be nested inside another CALCULATE. Nesting CALCULATE is a common pattern for applying multiple filter overrides.
choices: True
False
daxExpression:
-- FALSE: CALCULATE CAN be nested inside another CALCULATE
Nested Example =
    CALCULATE(
        CALCULATE(
            SUM(Sales[Amount]),
            Sales[Region] = "East"
        ),
        Sales[Year] = 2024
    )

-- The inner CALCULATE applies the Region filter.
-- The outer CALCULATE applies the Year filter.
-- Both filters are active simultaneously — nested CALCULATE is a valid and common pattern.

question: In a star schema, all dimension tables connect directly to the central fact table with no intermediate tables between them.
explanation: TRUE. In a star schema, all dimension tables have a direct relationship to the central fact table, with no intermediate tables.

False

question: In Power BI Import mode, the dataset reflects source changes in near-real-time without requiring a manual or scheduled refresh.

question: Row-level security (RLS) in Power BI is enforced at the semantic model level, meaning it applies to all reports and visuals built on that model regardless of how users access the data.
explanation: TRUE. RLS is defined on the semantic model and applies to every report and dashboard built on that model, regardless of where it is consumed.

False

question: A calculated column can be added to a slicer and used to filter report visuals, just like any imported column from the data source.
explanation: TRUE. Calculated columns are materialised at refresh time and behave identically to source columns — they can be used in slicers, filters, and visuals.

question: Contoso has 500 stores. Regional managers must see only their region data. Executives need a full unrestricted view in the same report. Which RLS design BEST meets both requirements?

parts.question: Which storage mode provides hourly data availability while handling the 200-million-row fact table most efficiently?
choices: Import mode with a 1-hour scheduled refresh
DirectQuery only on the fact table
DirectLake using Fabric OneLake
Composite model — Import for dimensions, DirectQuery for the fact table
parts.explanation: A composite model lets dimension tables use Import (fast slicer performance) while the large fact table uses DirectQuery (always reflects the latest data). Pure Import means a 60-minute data lag. Pure DirectQuery can be slow for aggregations across 200M rows. DirectLake requires Fabric OneLake infrastructure not mentioned in the scenario.

parts.question: Which Power BI feature ensures each regional manager sees only their region's data without requiring separate reports per region?
choices: Workspace Viewer role assigned per region
Row-level security with a USERPRINCIPALNAME() DAX filter
Sensitivity labels configured per regional report
One deployment pipeline stage per region
parts.explanation: Row-level security with USERPRINCIPALNAME() dynamically filters data based on the logged-in user's identity. A single model with a mapping table (user email → region) can serve all regional managers from one report. Workspace roles control workspace access, not row-level data visibility. Sensitivity labels classify data but do not filter rows.

choices: Create one static role per region with a hardcoded DAX filter for each region name
Create one dynamic role using USERPRINCIPALNAME() with a region-mapping table; assign executives to a separate role with no filter
Use workspace Viewer roles for managers and Member roles for executives to control data visibility
Apply Object-Level Security to hide non-relevant columns for each regional manager
explanation: A single dynamic role using USERPRINCIPALNAME() + a mapping table scales to all regions. Executives assigned to a separate unfiltered role see everything via Power BI union semantics. Static per-region roles require maintenance for every new region. Workspace roles control item access, not row visibility. OLS hides columns, not rows.

choiceExplanations.0: Creating one role per region means 500 roles to maintain — not scalable. Each new region requires a new role definition and model republish.
choiceExplanations.1: Correct. One dynamic role with USERPRINCIPALNAME() + a mapping table handles all regions without role proliferation. Executives in a separate unfiltered role see all data.
choiceExplanations.2: Workspace roles control who can access workspace items, not which rows a user sees within a dataset. RLS is required for row-level data restriction.
choiceExplanations.3: OLS hides entire columns from users — it cannot restrict a manager to specific region rows while showing all region columns.

subtopic: Create model calculations by using DAX
question: A DAX measure using SUMX returns 12,500 on a card visual but returns smaller values per row inside a matrix with product rows. The developer expected the same total everywhere. What is the MOST likely explanation?

parts.question: What type of context does SUMX create when it evaluates its expression argument?
choices: A filter context driven by the current slicer selections
A row context — it evaluates the expression independently for each row of the table
A query context derived from the visual's dimensions
A user security context based on the logged-in account
parts.explanation: SUMX is an iterator. It creates a row context by visiting each row of the specified table and evaluating the expression in that row's context. It then aggregates all row results. The filter context (from slicers, report filters, etc.) determines which rows are included before iteration begins.

parts.question: What does wrapping the SUMX expression inside CALCULATE fundamentally change about how the measure executes?
choices: The table that SUMX iterates over
The number of rows processed by SUMX
The filter context applied before SUMX begins iterating
The aggregation method from SUM to a weighted average
parts.explanation: CALCULATE modifies the filter context surrounding the SUMX evaluation. It does not change the iteration itself — SUMX still visits every row. However, CALCULATE changes which rows are visible before iteration begins. This explains why CALCULATE(SUMX(...)) can return a different value than SUMX(...) alone: the filter context differs.

choices: SUMX does not support matrix visuals — SUM should be used instead for tabular contexts
The matrix applies a row filter context for each product row, changing which rows SUMX iterates
Card visuals always ignore all active filters and always return the grand total
SUMX requires REMOVEFILTERS() to produce consistent results across different visual types
explanation: This is the correct and expected behaviour. Each matrix cell evaluates the measure in the filter context of that product row — SUMX only iterates rows for that product. The card has no additional row context so SUMX iterates all rows. This demonstrates filter context working as designed.

choiceExplanations.0: SUMX works correctly in matrix visuals. The per-row behaviour is expected and correct — it is the purpose of row context in a matrix.
choiceExplanations.1: Correct. Each matrix row adds a product filter context, so SUMX iterates only that product's rows. The card has no row context so it iterates all rows — hence different values.
choiceExplanations.2: Card visuals do respect filter context from slicers and page-level filters. They simply have no row context from matrix headers.
choiceExplanations.3: Adding REMOVEFILTERS would break the measure's responsiveness to all filters, including the matrix rows. The matrix behaviour is correct as-is and should not be changed.

daxExpression:
Total Revenue = SUMX(Sales, Sales[Qty] * Sales[UnitPrice])

-- On a card visual: no product filter → SUMX iterates ALL Sales rows → 12,500
-- On a matrix with Product on rows: each cell has a Product filter
--   → SUMX iterates only the Sales rows for THAT product
--   → Each cell shows that product's revenue (smaller than 12,500)

question: A Power BI team manages content across Development, Test, and Production workspaces. They need to promote reports through stages, compare differences between stages, and roll back if issues arise. Which feature BEST supports this?

parts.question: Which Power BI feature provides built-in Development → Test → Production stage management with content comparison and rollback visibility?
choices: Workspace Roles
Sensitivity Labels
Deployment Pipelines
Data Gateway configuration
parts.explanation: Power BI Deployment Pipelines provide a structured mechanism for promoting reports, dashboards, and semantic models across up to three pipeline stages. They include side-by-side comparison views and deployment history, making the process auditable and repeatable.

parts.question: A team member needs to deploy content from the Test stage to the Production workspace. What workspace role must they hold in the Production workspace to execute the deployment?
choices: Viewer role in the Production workspace
Contributor role in the Production workspace
Admin or Member role in the Production workspace
Any workspace role, as pipeline access is controlled separately
parts.explanation: Deploying to a pipeline stage requires at least Member role in the target workspace. Viewer and Contributor roles do not grant deployment permissions. Admin naturally has all permissions. Pipeline ownership alone is not sufficient — the workspace role in the destination must be Admin or Member.

choices: Manually publish the .pbix file from Power BI Desktop to each workspace separately
Use Power BI deployment pipelines to link three workspaces as Dev, Test, and Prod stages
Export reports as Power BI templates (.pbit) and import into each workspace as needed
Use the Power BI REST API to script item copies between workspaces
explanation: Deployment pipelines natively connect three workspaces as pipeline stages, provide a comparison view showing which items differ between stages, and support one-click promotion with automatic data source rebinding. They are purpose-built for this exact requirement.

choiceExplanations.0: Manual publishing has no comparison capability, no rollback, and no pipeline tracking. It is error-prone at scale and does not meet the comparison requirement.
choiceExplanations.1: Correct. Deployment pipelines link Dev, Test, and Prod workspaces, show item-level diff between stages, support selective deployment, and integrate with Premium/PPU capacity.
choiceExplanations.2: Templates export model schema and transformations but not the published report state or permissions. They do not support stage comparison or rollback.
choiceExplanations.3: The REST API can copy items programmatically but requires custom development and has no built-in comparison UI or managed rollback mechanism.

question: A Power BI report connected to a 15M-row fact table via DirectQuery averages 12-second load times. Performance Analyzer shows YTD and prior-year comparison calculated columns account for 9 seconds of Formula Engine time. What is the MOST effective optimization?
choices: Add composite indexes to the YTD and comparison columns in the source database
Convert the fact table to Import mode and rewrite the YTD and comparison logic as DAX time intelligence measures
Apply a report-level date filter limiting the visible range to 24 months
Switch to a composite model using DirectLake for the fact table
explanation: Calculated columns in DirectQuery mode are computed by the Formula Engine on every query — not stored in VertiPaq. With 15M rows, every YTD iteration is repeated per visual per page load. Converting to Import mode stores data in compressed columnar storage and time intelligence measures operate on pre-aggregated results, reducing Formula Engine work by orders of magnitude. DirectLake requires OneLake/Fabric, not arbitrary on-premises sources.

choiceExplanations.0: Adding composite indexes helps the database engine serve queries faster, but the bottleneck is the Power BI Formula Engine computing calculated columns on every query — not the database scan speed. Indexes won't fix Formula Engine overhead.
choiceExplanations.1: Correct. Calculated columns in DirectQuery mode are re-evaluated by the Formula Engine on every visual query against all 15M rows. Converting to Import stores data in VertiPaq (compressed columnar), and rewriting YTD/comparison logic as DAX measures evaluates against aggregated values — reducing Formula Engine work by orders of magnitude.
choiceExplanations.2: Reducing the visible date range reduces the rows processed by visuals, but the calculated columns still exist in the model and still force Formula Engine evaluation on the filtered row set. It is a partial workaround, not a root-cause fix.
choiceExplanations.3: DirectLake is a Microsoft Fabric storage mode that reads from OneLake parquet files with near-Import speed. It cannot connect to on-premises SQL Server and is not available in this architecture.

question: A Power BI model refresh takes 55 minutes and the PBIX file is 2.8 GB. The model contains a single denormalized fact table with 65 columns, including 20 high-cardinality string columns (Region, ProductName, CustomerTier, SubCategory, etc.) repeated across 40M rows. Which change will MOST reduce model size?
choices: Remove all calculated columns and replace them with measures
Enable incremental refresh on the fact table to reduce the data loaded
Convert the high-cardinality string dimension columns to integer foreign keys and move them into separate dimension tables
Change the fact table storage mode from Import to DirectQuery
explanation: VertiPaq compression is most effective on columns with low cardinality. Moving high-cardinality string columns (thousands of unique values) into dimension tables with integer foreign keys means the fact table stores compact integer keys instead of long strings repeated across 40M rows. This is the foundational benefit of the star schema pattern — dramatically better compression and faster query performance.

choiceExplanations.0: Removing calculated columns reduces Formula Engine overhead but does not directly reduce the number of rows or the cardinality of string columns stored in VertiPaq. The bloat comes from string repetition across 40M rows, not calculated columns.
choiceExplanations.1: Incremental refresh reduces the volume of data processed during each refresh cycle, but the full model — including all 65 columns — still exists in memory after load. It reduces refresh duration, not resident model size.
choiceExplanations.2: Correct. VertiPaq compresses by encoding repeated string values. High-cardinality strings repeated across 40M rows defeat this compression. Moving strings to integer foreign keys in a dimension table allows VertiPaq to store a single integer per fact row and compress the dimension's strings once — drastically reducing model size and improving refresh time.
choiceExplanations.3: Switching to DirectQuery removes the in-memory footprint, but also eliminates Import's query performance advantage, disables stored calculated columns, and places all query load on the source system. It does not reduce model size in a meaningful way — it eliminates the model.

question: A developer loads data from Azure SQL Database using Power Query. After a 'Merge Queries' step, they apply 'Remove Duplicates' then 'Sort Rows'. The model refresh takes 45 minutes despite the source table having only 2M rows. What is the MOST likely root cause?
choices: The Merge Queries step always performs a full table scan regardless of keys
Azure SQL Database has a query timeout that interrupts Power Query after 30 minutes
'Remove Duplicates' breaks query folding — all subsequent steps execute in-memory after downloading the full dataset to Power Query
Sort Rows forces a second connection to the database to re-read the data in order
explanation: Many Power Query operations cannot be translated to SQL and break the query folding chain — 'Remove Duplicates' is one of them. Once folding is broken, Power Query downloads the full dataset to its M engine in memory before applying subsequent steps. The fix: use DISTINCT in the source SQL query or ensure deduplication steps come before any transformations that break folding.

choiceExplanations.0: A Merge Queries step can generate a large SQL JOIN, but the query itself would still fold to the database if no non-foldable steps precede it. The join alone does not explain a 45-minute refresh for 2M rows.
choiceExplanations.1: Azure SQL Database timeouts are typically 30 seconds to a few minutes, not 45 minutes. The behavior described — a slow but eventually completing refresh — does not match an interrupted timeout pattern.
choiceExplanations.2: Correct. 'Remove Duplicates' in Power Query uses an in-memory hash set operation that cannot be translated to SQL — it breaks query folding. Once folding breaks, Power Query downloads the full dataset to local memory before applying any subsequent steps. For 2M rows this is extremely slow compared to server-side processing.
choiceExplanations.3: Sort Rows can fold to SQL as an ORDER BY clause if folding is intact. It does not open a second connection. However, because 'Remove Duplicates' already broke folding, Sort Rows runs in memory anyway.

tables.name: Query folding chain from Azure SQL
rows: Joins across queries may break folding
Cannot be pushed to SQL — fold chain breaks here
Downstream of fold break = in-memory only

question: Performance Analyzer shows a matrix visual takes 5,800ms to render. Storage Engine queries account for 180ms and the Formula Engine accounts for 5,620ms. What does this distribution indicate, and what should be investigated first?
choices: The matrix has too many rows — reduce visual cardinality by adding slicers
The model should switch to DirectQuery to bypass the Formula Engine bottleneck
The DAX measure uses complex iterators or nested CALCULATE calls that cannot be parallelised — rewrite using simpler aggregations or pre-aggregated calculated columns where appropriate
The underlying database is responding slowly — add indexes to the source system
explanation: The Formula Engine (single-threaded DAX evaluation) dominates when VertiPaq cannot pre-aggregate the result. This pattern — low Storage Engine time, very high Formula Engine time — points to iterator functions (SUMX, RANKX over large tables), deeply nested CALCULATE chains, or context transition inside iterators. Switching to DirectQuery would send these same complex calculations as SQL, typically making performance worse, not better.

choiceExplanations.0: Reducing row count (adding slicers) would primarily reduce Storage Engine query time — the time to retrieve data. The Storage Engine is only 180ms here; reducing cardinality would have minimal impact on the 5,620ms Formula Engine bottleneck.
choiceExplanations.1: Switching to DirectQuery moves computation to the source database but does not fix poor DAX measure design. Complex DAX patterns like nested CALCULATE with iterators perform even worse in DirectQuery because the Formula Engine still runs and the Storage Engine now sends live SQL queries instead of reading from memory.
choiceExplanations.2: Correct. When the Formula Engine time vastly exceeds Storage Engine time, the DAX measure itself is the bottleneck — not data volume or source speed. This pattern indicates complex iterator logic, nested CALCULATE calls, or context transitions that cannot be parallelised. The fix is to rewrite the measure using simpler aggregations or pre-aggregate results in a calculated column where appropriate.
choiceExplanations.3: The Storage Engine (180ms) handles source queries and VertiPaq scans. At 180ms, the source is responding quickly — adding database indexes would not meaningfully reduce the 5,620ms Formula Engine time.

tables.name: Performance Analyzer breakdown
rows: SE retrieves data from the compressed column store quickly
FE executes complex DAX — cannot be parallelised by SE
Optimize the DAX measure — reduce nested CALCULATE or iterators

subtopic: Choose between DirectLake, DirectQuery, and Import
question: A company requires Power BI reports to reflect database changes within 10 minutes during business hours. The source is Azure SQL Database. A full Import refresh takes 3 hours due to the 500M-row table size. What is the MOST appropriate solution?
choices: Schedule a full Import refresh every 10 minutes — Power BI Premium supports up to 48 refreshes per day
Use full DirectQuery mode so all queries go directly to Azure SQL with no refresh required
Configure hybrid tables with incremental refresh — keep recent partitions (last 7 days) in DirectQuery mode for near-real-time access while historical partitions remain in Import mode
Use streaming datasets with Azure Event Hubs to push data changes directly to Power BI
explanation: Hybrid tables (Power BI Premium) partition the table so recent data (e.g., last 7 days) is served via DirectQuery — always current — while historical data remains in Import mode for fast analytical performance. This avoids the cost of refreshing 500M rows every 10 minutes and provides the required recency. Full DirectQuery on a 500M-row analytical table (B, C) would produce very slow report performance. Streaming datasets are for real-time dashboards, not analytical reports.

choiceExplanations.0: Power BI Premium supports up to 48 scheduled refreshes per day. However, a 3-hour full refresh cycle cannot run every 10 minutes — the next refresh would start before the previous one completes. This approach is architecturally impossible for a 500M-row table.
choiceExplanations.1: Full DirectQuery mode provides live query access, but with a 500M-row table, complex analytical queries would perform extremely poorly. Every visual interaction generates a SQL query against 500M rows, making the dashboard unusable for analytical reporting.
choiceExplanations.2: Correct. Hybrid tables combine incremental refresh with DirectQuery on the most recent partition. Historical partitions remain as fast Import data in VertiPaq. The most recent partition (e.g., last 7 days) uses DirectQuery, providing near-real-time access without refreshing the entire 500M-row table. This is the purpose-built solution for this exact scenario.
choiceExplanations.3: Streaming datasets with Event Hubs push real-time event data to Power BI and work well for IoT or operational dashboards. They are not designed for querying a large transactional SQL database — they receive pushed events and do not replace scheduled or incremental refresh of existing relational data.

question: You implement RLS with the DAX filter `[Email] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()` on a Region dimension table. Regional managers report seeing data from all regions despite the filter. The Region table has a one-to-many relationship to the Sales fact table. Cross-filter direction is Single. What is the MOST likely cause?
choices: The Single cross-filter is set so Sales filters Region (Sales → Region), meaning the RLS filter on Region does not propagate to restrict Sales rows
USERPRINCIPALNAME() returns a domain-qualified name that does not match the Email column format
RLS filters must be placed on the fact table, not the dimension table
The one-to-many relationship cardinality is incorrectly configured
explanation: For RLS on a dimension table to restrict fact table rows, the cross-filter direction must flow from dimension to fact (Region → Sales). If the Single direction is set to Sales → Region, filters applied to Region do not propagate downstream to Sales — managers see all Sales rows. The fix: reverse the filter direction so Region can filter Sales, or set direction to Both.

choiceExplanations.0: Correct. With Single cross-filter direction and the filter set on the Region dimension, filters must flow FROM Region TO Sales for RLS to work. If the Single direction is set so Sales filters Region (fact to dimension), the RLS filter on Region cannot propagate downstream to restrict Sales rows. The fix is to reverse the filter direction so Region can filter Sales, or set direction to Both.
choiceExplanations.1: USERPRINCIPALNAME() format mismatch is a valid RLS issue in some scenarios, but it would affect ALL regional managers consistently, not cause them to see data from all regions. The question states all regions are visible — indicating the filter propagation is the problem, not the identity lookup.
choiceExplanations.2: RLS filters can be placed on any table — fact or dimension. Placing the filter on a dimension table is correct and standard when the intent is to propagate restrictions to the fact table via the relationship. The issue is the cross-filter direction, not which table holds the filter.
choiceExplanations.3: The one-to-many cardinality is correctly configured (one region to many sales). Incorrect cardinality would manifest as data quality issues such as wrong aggregations, not a complete bypass of RLS filtering where all regions are visible.

relationshipDiagram.issue: Cross-filter direction is Single (Sales → Region). RLS filter on Region does NOT propagate down to restrict Sales rows. Changing direction to "Single (Region → Sales)" fixes this.

question: A large organisation implements dynamic RLS using the filter on an Employees table: `[Department] IN SELECTCOLUMNS(FILTER(DeptAccess, [ManagerUPN] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()), "Dept", [Department])`. Senior managers report seeing no data. The DeptAccess table has no model relationship. What is the MOST likely cause?
choices: SELECTCOLUMNS cannot be used inside an RLS DAX expression
A model relationship must exist between DeptAccess and Employees for the filter to evaluate
The filter should be applied to the DeptAccess table rather than the Employees table

USERPRINCIPALNAME() returns the manager's email in a different case or domain format than stored in DeptAccess[ManagerUPN], causing FILTER to return an empty table — SELECTCOLUMNS then returns an empty set, matching no departments
explanation: The most common cause of 'no data visible' when the DAX syntax is correct is a UPN mismatch — the value USERPRINCIPALNAME() returns (e.g., 'Manager@contoso.com') doesn't exactly match DeptAccess[ManagerUPN] (e.g., 'manager@CONTOSO.COM'). FILTER returns an empty table, SELECTCOLUMNS returns no departments, and IN matches nothing. The fix: use LOWER() on both sides of the comparison. Disconnected tables work correctly in RLS filter expressions.

choiceExplanations.0: SELECTCOLUMNS is a valid table function in DAX and is supported in RLS expressions. It is commonly used in IN SELECTCOLUMNS(...) patterns for complex RLS scenarios. This is not the cause of the issue.
choiceExplanations.1: FILTER and SELECTCOLUMNS can operate on any table in the model regardless of whether a relationship exists. DAX table functions traverse the model without requiring physical relationships — unlike RELATED, which does. No relationship is required for this pattern to work.
choiceExplanations.2: The filter is correctly placed on the Employees table — that is the table that must be restricted. Placing it on DeptAccess would restrict access to DeptAccess rows, not Employee rows.
choiceExplanations.3: Correct. USERPRINCIPALNAME() returns the signed-in user's email. If the format or case in DeptAccess[ManagerUPN] does not exactly match (e.g., 'Jane@CONTOSO.COM' vs 'jane@contoso.com', or a domain alias vs primary UPN), FILTER returns an empty table. SELECTCOLUMNS on an empty table returns an empty column, so the IN check matches no departments — returning no rows to the manager. This is a common, subtle RLS failure mode.

daxExpression:
-- RLS filter on Employees table:
[Department] IN
    SELECTCOLUMNS(
        FILTER(
            DeptAccess,
            [ManagerUPN] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()
        ),
        "Dept", [Department]
    )

-- USERPRINCIPALNAME() = "Jane@CONTOSO.COM"  (case/domain from Azure AD)
-- DeptAccess[ManagerUPN] = "jane@contoso.com" (lowercase, stored manually)
-- FILTER result: 0 rows  →  SELECTCOLUMNS returns empty column
-- IN empty set  →  no rows returned  →  senior manager sees no data

expectedOutput.label: Execution trace — Jane signs in as Jane@CONTOSO.COM
rows: No rows — senior manager sees blank report

question: A Power BI model has an RLS role filtering the Product dimension table. A report shows product sales correctly filtered. However, a matrix visual showing 'Products with no sales this period' still shows products from other regions. Why does the RLS filter not restrict this visual?
choices: The matrix visual requires a separate RLS role defined specifically for that visual type
The 'Products with no sales' visual uses CROSSFILTER or a DAX measure that explicitly bypasses the Product filter — or the visual uses ALL(Product) to show unfiltered product members
Inactive relationships used by the visual bypass RLS enforcement
RLS filters on dimension tables do not apply to matrix visuals
explanation: RLS applies to all table reads consistently. A visual showing 'products with no sales' that ignores RLS is almost always using a DAX measure or visual configuration that removes or bypasses the Product filter — such as ALL(Product), REMOVEFILTERS, or CROSSFILTER in the measure definition. The RLS filter itself is functioning correctly; the measure is explicitly overriding it. Reviewing the measure DAX is the correct first step.

choiceExplanations.0: RLS in Power BI is enforced at the semantic model level, not at the visual type level. All visual types — including matrix visuals — are subject to the same RLS filter. No separate role per visual type exists or is needed.
choiceExplanations.1: Correct. The most likely explanation is that the 'Products with no sales' visual uses a DAX measure or visual configuration that explicitly removes the Product table filter — for example, using ALL(Product) in a measure, or a CROSSFILTER call that detaches Product from the active filter context. If the measure uses ALL(Product), RLS on the Product dimension table is bypassed because the measure itself removes the filter that RLS added.
choiceExplanations.2: Inactive relationships are not used by default — they require USERELATIONSHIP to activate. An inactive relationship would not cause extra products to appear; it would cause measures using that relationship to return BLANK.
choiceExplanations.3: RLS filters on dimension tables DO apply to matrix visuals. The visual type does not determine whether RLS is enforced. If RLS were bypassed by default for matrix visuals, it would be a critical platform-level security vulnerability.

daxExpression:
-- The visual may use a measure that explicitly bypasses the Product filter:
-- Example that would cause this:
All Products in Category =
    CALCULATE(
        COUNTROWS(Products),
        ALL(Products)   -- bypasses RLS filter on Product table
    )

-- RLS filters are enforced at table read time.
-- A measure using ALL(Product), REMOVEFILTERS, or CROSSFILTER
-- can override the RLS-applied filter in specific calculations.

question: A company wants an external contractor to create new reports using the organisation's shared semantic model but must not be able to modify the existing published reports in the workspace. Which permission assignment is MOST appropriate?
choices: Assign Contributor role in the workspace so the contractor can publish new content
Assign Member role in the workspace with restricted dataset access
Grant Build permission on the semantic model only — the contractor can create new reports in their own workspace from the shared model but cannot edit reports in the shared workspace
Assign Viewer role in the workspace and enable Content Pack distribution
explanation: Build permission on a semantic model allows users to create new reports from that model in their own workspace without requiring any workspace role on the shared workspace. Contributor role (B) allows creating AND editing all content in the workspace — more access than required. Viewer role (C) cannot publish content at all. Member role (D) provides even broader access than Contributor.

choiceExplanations.0: Contributor role grants the ability to publish new content AND edit existing reports and datasets in the workspace. This exceeds the requirement — the contractor must not be able to modify existing published reports.
choiceExplanations.1: Member role provides full content management capabilities including managing workspace app and adding Members or lower roles. This is far more access than required and still allows editing existing reports.
choiceExplanations.2: Correct. Build permission on a semantic model allows a user to create new reports connected to that model in their own workspace without requiring any workspace role on the shared workspace. This is the purpose-built permission for external report builders who should not touch existing workspace content.
choiceExplanations.3: Viewer role provides read-only access to the workspace and does not allow the contractor to publish new reports. Content Pack distribution is a legacy feature, not applicable to this scenario.

subtopic: Design and implement a data model
question: A retail model has two fact tables: OnlineSales and StoreSales. Both need to relate to the same Date, Customer, and Product dimension tables. A many-to-many relationship naturally exists between Products and Promotions (one product can have multiple promotions; one promotion can cover multiple products). What is the correct modeling pattern for the Product-Promotion relationship?
choices: Create a direct bidirectional many-to-many relationship between Product and Promotion
Add a PromotionKey foreign key directly to the Product dimension table
